presentations.presentation_title: Energy Transfer Via Wave Particle Interactions at Mars: Statistical Study Over 10 Years of MAVEN Data
presentations.abstract: Wave-particle interactions are an important physical process that can govern particle dynamics of charged particles in planetary magnetospheres. Magnetic pumping is an example of such a process that allows the transfer of energy from ultra-low frequency waves at magnetohydrodynamical scales to ambient electrons in planetary environments at kinetic scales. As these waves propagate through the system they can drive significant heating of ambient plasma, coupling the magnetosphere to the solar wind. This has been observed at Mars and Venus in their ionospheres, and these observations form the motivation for this study. Here we focus on magnetic pumping at Mars. The underlying ULF waves are driven by the solar wind interaction with the planet, with magnetic pumping and subsequent heating of ambient electrons observed in the dayside ionosphere. The process thus couples the solar wind to the planetary ionosphere. NASAs Mars Atmosphere and Volatile EvolutioN (MAVEN) mission has orbited Mars over one complete solar cycle, allowing statistical studies to investigate changes in the Martian system over nearly 12 years of data. This study looks at the likelihood of occurrence of magnetic pumping as a function of position in the Martian magnetosphere, and external drivers such as season and solar wind conditions. Identifying regions and times where magnetic pumping is more likely can determine where solar wind energy is transferred to the ionospheric electrons. Such knowledge may have important implications for processes such as ionospheric dynamics, heating and subsequent loss into space.

presentations.presentation_title: Effects of an Intrinsic Magnetic Field on Ion Escape From Ancient Mars Based on MAESTRO Multifluid MHD Simulation
presentations.abstract: Ion escape is one of the key processes driving atmospheric loss on ancient Mars due to strong solar activity. However, the presence of a global intrinsic magnetic field on ancient Mars affected solar wind-Mars interactions and ion escape. Differential flows between ion species can also be important for ion escape in the presence of a strong intrinsic magnetic field, where cusp outflows dominate. In this study, we investigated the role of the intrinsic magnetic field in ion escape from ancient Mars using a new global multifluid MHD model with a cubed sphere grid system, named MAESTRO (Multifluid Atmospheric Escape Simulations Toward Real elucidatiOn). We conducted a series of multifluid MHD simulations with varying only dipole field strengths. We also performed multispecies single-fluid MHD simulations under the same conditions to assess the effects of differential flows. The multifluid cases exhibit asymmetric outflow distributions with respect to the solar wind electric field, consistent with previous studies. They also show higher escape rates of molecular ions (O 2 + and CO 2 + ) than the multispecies cases, indicating that the single-fluid approximation underestimates ion outflows from the ionosphere. This effect is pronounced in the strong-dipole-field cases, where the escape rates are more than two orders of magnitude higher. The O + escape rate is also higher by an order of magnitude in the strongest dipole field case. In contrast, the multifluid representation slightly reduces the O + escape rates in the no- or weak-dipole-field cases due to the suppression of pickup-like escape in the –E hemisphere. The presence of a strong dipole field reduces the total escape rate of heavy ions by a factor of six. The impacts on atmospheric escape are diminished but remain significant. This study also highlights the importance of a multifluid modeling approach in evaluating ion escape from magnetized planets.

presentations.presentation_title: Study of the Spatial Distribution of Martian Diffuse Aurora Caused by Sep Electron Precipitation During the September 2017 Icme Event Based on Ptrip and Maestro Models
presentations.institution: Department of Earth and Planetary Science, Graduate School of Science, The University of Tokyo
presentations.abstract: Solar Energetic Particles (SEP) from solar flares and interplanetary coronal mass ejections (ICME) trigger diffuse aurora when they precipitate into the Martian atmosphere. During the September 2017 ICME event, MAVEN/IUVS observed dramatic morphological variations in auroral emissions: a “global” emission at 9/13 10:00 UT transitioned to a “northern-hemisphere-dominated” emission at 9/14 03:44 UT (Schneider et al., 2018). The physical mechanism driving this rapid transition remains unidentified. Given that SEP electrons have smaller gyroradii than protons, they are highly sensitive to localized magnetic field configurations, making them the primary candidate for driving such dynamic auroral variations. In this study, we aim to reproduce the morphological transition in the diffuse auroral emission distribution during the 13-14 September 2017 event. We performed statistical trajectory tracings of electrons using PTRIP (Nakamura et al., 2022) under magnetic field configurations simulated by the global multispecies magnetohydrodynamics model MAESTRO (Sakata et al., 2024). We here traced electron trajectories backward in time from the 300-km altitude sphere with 10º latitude and longitude resolutions to derive SEP electron precipitation maps at the altitude. At each location, initial pitch and phase angles are set to have full coverage with 10º and 36º resolutions. The results show that there are two source regions of precipitating SEP electrons, i.e., the sunward and anti-sunward sources. The global precipitation rate of 100-keV electrons onto the 300-km altitude changed from 63 to 40 % during the transition. The model qualitatively reproduced the observed morphological transition from "global" precipitation on September 13 to "northern-hemisphere-dominated" precipitation on September 14. The results also suggest that North-South asymmetry on September 14 was caused by suppressed southern precipitation, stemming from closed magnetic field configuration formed by nightside magnetic reconnection. A quantitative comparison of auroral emission intensity with the MAVEN/IUVS observations will be also reported.

presentations.presentation_title: Discovery of Heavy Ion Aurora at Mars
presentations.institution: University of Colorado, Boulder, Laboratory for Atmospheric and Space Physics
presentations.abstract: We report here on the discovery of a new type of Martian aurora produced by the precipitation of heavy ions during highly dynamic space weather events. Auroral emissions excited by heavy ions have a signature of atomic emissions characteristic of the precipitating ions and their neutral counterparts as repeated charge exchange reactions occur in the upper atmosphere. In other words, the precipitating particles themselves emit photons instead of simply exciting the atmosphere they travel through. This is the same process by which the related phenomenon of proton aurora are produced. The detectability of heavy ion aurora depends on having favorable cross-sections for emission at the energy of the precipitating particles, as well as an ability to distinguish the emitted photons from other excitation processes. Using a combination of remote sensing and in-situ data from the MAVEN and EMM orbiter missions, we have identified multiple events on both the dayside and nightside when unusually bright atomic oxygen and carbon emissions occurred in association with enhanced heavy ion precipitation. During these events other atomic and molecular emissions typically associated with electron and proton aurora at Mars were either very weak or uncorrelated in time and location. We will discuss how heavy ion precipitation contributes to explaining the wide range of Martian auroral phenomena actively being characterized, along with a brief review of past work done for Earth and Jupiter and its relevance and implications for Mars. Mechanisms in the Martian magnetosphere capable of generating heavy ions energetic enough to produce aurora, such as pickup ions, will be reviewed. Finally, we will address the implications for atmospheric evolution, in particular studying atmospheric sputtering.

presentations.presentation_title: Statistical Study of Ion Escape from Mars During CIR Events Based on Maven Observations
presentations.abstract: Mars lacks a global intrinsic magnetic field and is directly exposed to the solar wind, making its atmosphere vulnerable to ion escape. Space weather events such as coronal mass ejections (CMEs) and corotating interaction regions (CIRs) often enhance solar wind dynamic pressure and disturb the Martian induced magnetosphere. While several studies have reported increased ion escape rates during CMEs (e.g., Jakosky et al., 2015), a statistical study found no clear dependence on solar wind dynamic pressure (Ramstad et al., 2018). These contradictory results motivate further investigation. In this study, we focus on CIRs, for which enough events are available for a statistical analysis, and evaluate their effects on ion escape based on observations.Utilizing solar wind parameters observed by MAVEN from 2014 to 2023, we identified 130 CIR events. We then examined the spatial distributions of heavy ion fluxes during both CIR periods and the entire observation period. The results show that the spatial distributions of median heavy ion fluxes during the CIR periods are similar to those of the entire period, while observation frequencies of high outward fluxes above mean values plus ~2σ are increased during CIRs. The high fluxes were often observed in the tail region on the dusk side in the Mars–Solar–Orbital (MSO) coordinate system, while the spatial asymmetry in the Mars-Solar-Electric field (MSE) coordinate system was relatively small. When separating events by IMF orientation and the location of crustal magnetic fields, we found that toward IMF cases show a stronger dawn–dusk asymmetry than away IMF cases, while no significant differences is found among different locations of crustal magnetic fields. A comparison of these results with MHD simulations (Sakata et al., 2024) suggests that the observed dawn–dusk asymmetry may be related to open magnetic field lines particularly connected to the dayside ionosphere.

presentations.presentation_title: Juno Microwave Radiometer Observations of the Subsurface of Io, Europa and Ganymede
presentations.abstract: On June 7, 2021, and September 29, 2022, the NASA Juno spacecraft passed Jupiter’s Galilean moons, Ganymede, and Europa, respectively. On December 23, 2023 and February 3, 2024, Juno passed Jupiter’s Galilean moon Io. The closest approach distance was ~1000 km above Ganymede, and ~350 km above Europa and ~1500 km above Io. The close flybys were the first encounters with the moons in over two decades and provided the first opportunity to map the subsurface ice shells at multiple microwave frequencies using Juno’s Microwave Radiometer (MWR). The observations provided several swaths across both moons at six frequencies, ranging from 600 MHz to 22 GHz. The ice transparency at microwave frequencies is dependent on purity; assuming pure ice, the observations probe depths ranging from meters to kilometers. The MWR observations represent the first resolved interrogation of Ganymede and Europa’s subsurface ice shell revealing new constraints on porosity, fracturing, differences in terrain type and possibly the thickness of the conductive ice shell. These unprecedented measurements on Io, Europa and Ganymede will provide new insights into the comparative nature of the surfaces and interiors of the Jovian satellites. The Juno MWR measurements complement previous ground-based radar and microwave radiometry observations which provided early characterization of these icy satellite surfaces. A comparison of the microwave spectra for all three satellites will be presented as well as a detailed analysis and interpretation of the Ganymede MWR data that provide new constraints on ice subsurface properties.

presentations.presentation_title: Juno Microwave Radiometer Measurements of the Depths of Spatial and Temporal Variability in Jupiter
presentations.institution: Jet Propulsion Laboratory, California Institute of Technology
presentations.abstract: Juno’s Microwave Radiometer (MWR) provides an unprecedented opportunity to explore the dynamics and composition of Jupiter’s deep atmosphere. Since Juno’s arrival in 2016, the MWR has observed microwave emission at wavelengths between 1.3 and 50 cm, sensing from 0.7 bar to over 100 bars of pressure, at over 75 close approaches to the atmosphere. A concerted effort has collected MWR-supporting contextual information from other Juno instruments, as well as ground- and space-based observations, sensing the upper atmosphere at complementary wavelengths. Among the MWR’s results are observations of long-term variability in Jupiter over 2016-2025. The North Equatorial Belt, (NEB: 12°N-16°N) shows the greatest variability. The strongest variability associated with discrete features in the atmosphere is a major upwelling and subsequent clearing of cloud cover in the North Temperate Belt (NTB: 20°N-26°N) in August-September of 2020. The microwave brightness-temperature variability often correlates with visible variability. In some regions, such as the Equatorial Zone (EZ: 3°S-6°N), substantial variability is detected both in regions above the level of the water-condensate cloud (~10 bars) but also at great depth. In general, 5-µm brightness temperatures, largely modulated by cloud cover, are anticorrelated with MWR brightness temperatures, consistent with an upward motion in a stably stratified atmosphere that decreases NH 3 vapor with altitude. NEB and NTB disturbances are most likely to be caused by baroclinic instabilities that grow fast, return to their initial unperturbed state more slowly and require a lateral density contrast. They do not affect the atmosphere significantly below the H 2 O condensation level. In contrast, the EZ disturbances extend deeper in the atmosphere and are likely to be caused by convective instability, which is more symmetric between its growth and decaying phases and requires a vertical entropy contrast.

presentations.presentation_title: Lunar Surface Dielectric Characterization from 100 GHz Polarization Ratios Observed by the Nobeyama 45‑m Telescope
presentations.institution: National Institute of Information and Communications Technology
presentations.abstract: We conducted polarization measurements of the Moon at about 100 GHz using the Nobeyama 45‑m radio telescope to evaluate the feasibility of deriving lunar surface dielectric properties from millimeter-wave observations. Vertical (V) and horizontal (H) brightness temperatures were independently calibrated, and the resulting V/H intensity ratio was analyzed as a function of emission angle. The ratio systematically increases toward the limb, consistent with expectations from emissivity differences predicted by Fresnel equations for a dielectric surface. Preliminary results demonstrate that single-scan polarization measurements have the potential to constrain the dielectric properties of the lunar surface, and further analysis will investigate their applicability to mapping geological diversity.

presentations.presentation_title: Téraherz Heterodyne Receivers Technology for Planetary Science
presentations.abstract: Both interstellar medium and planetary atmospheres are incredibly rich in molecular species with spectral rotational and vibrational signatures that lie in the 0.3-5 THz frequency range. Submillimeter and terahertz heterodyne receivers allow us not only to trace minor and major molecular species but also their dynamics. Both super- and semiconductor technology development foster the deployment of these space born high spectral resolution instruments in the Terahertz frequency range. In this presentation we shall focus on the recent developments at LIRA-Observatoire de Paris based on Schottky semiconductor technology for the generation and detection of frequencies up to 2THz in the frame of the preparation of space missions such as AOS, LIGHTSHIP/ZEFERO, KEYSTONE.

presentations.presentation_title: Geometric Control of Surface Charging on Airless Bodies: Cavities, Particle Layers, and Lunar Pits
presentations.abstract: Surface charging on airless planetary bodies is set by the balance of electron and ion currents from the surrounding plasma. Classical charging models often assume open, planar surfaces, but real topography can geometrically restrict particle access and thereby alter the current balance. We quantify this geometric control using three-dimensional electrostatic particle-in-cell (PIC) simulations across a hierarchy of near-surface structures: (i) idealized cavities, (ii) particle-layer configurations with interstitial gaps, and (iii) pit-like geometries motivated by lunar skylights.When the characteristic size of a geometrically confined structure becomes comparable to or smaller than the local Debye length, electron access to the interior is selectively suppressed, whereas ions can still penetrate owing to their larger inertia. This accessibility asymmetry produces an ion-dominated current balance and generates positive electrostatic potentials even under solar-wind conditions that would charge open planar surfaces negatively. Once in the sub-Debye regime, the resulting potential structure shows only weak sensitivity to further reductions in size or to detailed geometric shape.Particle-layer simulations exhibit localized positive charging within narrow gaps between surface particles despite the absence of carved cavities, demonstrating that the same mechanism operates across distinct morphologies. Preliminary pit-like simulations indicate similar electron-access limitations and ion-dominated charging in vertically confined structures, supporting the robustness of geometric control from idealized to realistic topography.These results highlight geometric confinement as a key regulator of surface-plasma coupling and near-surface electrostatic environments on the Moon, Mercury, and small bodies exposed directly to the solar wind.

presentations.presentation_title: Heating of the Upper Atmospheres of Mars and Titan by Acoustic-gravity Wave Dissipation
presentations.institution: State Key Laboratory of Lunar and Planetary Sciences, Macau University of Science and Technology
presentations.abstract: Recent spacecraft observations have revealed pronounced and highly variable thermal structures in the upper atmospheres of Mars and Titan, indicating the presence of efficient wave-driven energy transport and dissipation processes. Acoustic–gravity waves (AGWs), which are ubiquitous in planetary atmospheres, can propagate upward from lower atmospheric sources and dissipate through molecular viscosity and thermal conduction, thereby modifying the thermal balance of the upper atmosphere. We investigate AGW-induced heating and cooling in the upper atmospheres of Mars and Titan using linear wave models. We show that wave-driven thermal effects are primarily governed by the sensible heat flux, which depends critically on the amplitude and phase relationship between vertical velocity and temperature perturbations, with viscous dissipation becoming increasingly important at higher altitudes. High-frequency acoustic waves exhibit nearly in-phase velocity and temperature perturbations, resulting in efficient upward sensible heat transport and net heating of the upper atmosphere. On Mars, the associated heating rates can reach several hundred Kelvin per Martian day. Gravity waves exhibit more complex behavior. In the lower atmosphere, partial phase alignment between velocity and temperature perturbations leads to upward sensible heat transport and localized heating. As gravity waves propagate to higher altitudes, enhanced molecular viscosity and thermal conduction shift the temperature phase beyond 90° relative to the vertical velocity, causing downward energy deposition. Consequently, gravity waves tend to cool the upper atmosphere while heating lower regions. For Titan, acoustic waves consistently produce heating, with maximum heating rates of up to 80 K day⁻¹ and exobase temperature increases of up to 22 K, enhancing the Jeans escape flux of molecular hydrogen by 3–24%. Gravity waves with high phase speeds contribute to heating, whereas slower gravity waves predominantly cool the upper atmosphere and reduce atmospheric escape.

presentations.presentation_title: Discrete Energy Bands Beyond Galilean Moons: Bounce-phase Structuring of Jovian Magnetospheric Particles
presentations.abstract: Discrete energy bands of ion fluxes, typically organized in velocity with equal separations, have been frequently observed in Jupiter’s magnetosphere either in association with Galilean moons or in regions far from their influence. Here, we focus on the latter and propose that these bands are manifestations of bounce-phase structuring, analogous to drift-phase structuring responsible for the well-known zebra-stripe patterns. In our proposed framework, latitude-dependent electric-field perturbations interact with ions at different bounce phases, producing phase-dependent energy modulations. As the ions continue to bounce at their respective bounce frequencies, which scale with ion velocity, these modulations naturally evolve into discrete, velocity-ordered banded structures. We examine several potential sources of latitude-dependent electric fields, including impulsive disturbances and wave-related processes. Test-particle simulations reproduce the key observational features. These results support bounce-phase structuring as a unifying interpretation of both non-moon and moon-associated discrete bands, and provide a new diagnostic perspective on Jovian magnetospheric dynamics.

presentations.presentation_title: Updated Status and Upcoming Plans of the Bepicolombo Mission
presentations.institution: Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency / Institute of Space and Astronautical Science
presentations.abstract: BepiColombo is a joint mission between the European Space Agency (ESA) and the Japanese Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA), to will carry out a comprehensive exploration of planet Mercury. The mission was launched on 20 October 2018 and is still on an eight-year-long cruise to Mercury. BepiColombo consists of two orbiters: the Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) and the Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (Mio). Following their release from the Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) in September 2026, these orbiters will be put in orbit around the innermost planet of our Solar System in November 2026. The nominal science phase will start in April 2027 and BepiColombo with its very comprehensive and interdisciplinary payloads will perform measurements to increase our knowledge on the fundamental questions about Mercury’s evolution, composition, interior, magnetosphere, and exosphere. BepiColombo successfully completed the last of its 6 flybys of Mercury in January 2025. Although the two BepiColombo orbiters are in a stacked configuration during the cruise, during which only some of the instruments can perform scientific observations, the mission has already produced some very valuable results, including striking observations of the planet using its three engineering monitoring cameras. We shall provide a summary of the mission status, a preview of the remaining plans for the mission up to and after arrival in orbit around Mercury, and a broad overview of scientific results to date.

presentations.presentation_title: The Submillimetre Wave Instrument (SWI) on Juice: Spacecraft Outgassing Detection and Interpretation
presentations.institution: Max Planck Institute for Solar System Research
presentations.abstract: The Submillimeter Wave Instrument (SWI) is part of the payload of ESA’s L1 mission JUICE (JUpiter ICy moons Explorer). It sounds the atmospheres of Jupiter and the Galilean moons in two Far Infrared bands covering the frequency ranges of 530 – 625 GHz and 1065 – 1280 GHz. Furthermore, it is designed to characterize the thermo-physical surface properties of Callisto, Ganymede and Europa during flyby and orbital phases. After the successful launch in April 2023 and the commissioning of the instrument, several payload checkout windows and flybys provided a lot of interesting data, including water outgassing of the spacecraft. The presentation will focus on results from the Lunar Earth Gravity Assist.

presentations.presentation_title: Radiative Transfer Calculation for Lunar Subsurface Observation with JUCE/SWI
presentations.abstract: Lunar exploration missions are currently increasing in preparation for future human activities on the Moon. A terahertz remote sensing mission, the Lunar Terahertz SUrveyor for KIlometer-scale MappIng (TSUKIMI), is being planned to investigate subsurface water ice with 0.3 and 0.5 THz bands. Similar observations of the lunar surface and subsurface were carried out during the Moon–Earth flyby of the JUICE mission using the Submillimetre Wave Instrument (SWI) with 0.6 and 1.2 THz bands, providing a unique opportunity to study thermal emission. In this study, we present the development of a one-dimensional multilayer radiative transfer model to describe the propagation and emission of terahertz radiation in the lunar subsurface. The model considers multiple regolith layers with different physical and dielectric properties and is applicable to the frequency ranges relevant to both TSUKIMI and JUICE/SWI. This work represents a physical framework for radiative transfer calculation in the lunar subsurface in the terahertz frequency region, aimed at supporting for future global observation. Model simulations of brightness temperature are compared with measurements obtained by JUICE/SWI in order to evaluate the capability of the model to reproduce the observed large-scale characteristics of lunar thermal emission. A quantitative assessment of the agreement between simulations and observations and their implications for the interpretation of terahertz lunar observations will be presented and discussed.

presentations.presentation_title: Molecular Gas Outflow Activity Of The Interstellar Comet 3I/ATLAS
presentations.abstract: 3I/ATLAS, the 2 nd interstellar comet ever discovered by humans, was reported on 2025 July 1, and reached the perihelion four months later on October 29. We employed the 15m (sub)millimeter-wave James Clerk Maxwell Telescope to monitor 3I/ATLAS activity throughout its inner Solar-System journey, from early August to December of 2025, for five months, covering both pre-perihelion and post-perihelion phases of the comet. HCN outgassing was first detected on September 14 at a heliocentric distance of 2.13 AU (CBET 5608); multiple transitions of CH 3 OH emission were also first detected at a heliocentric distance of 1.39 AU on October 20 (CBET 5628). In this presentation, I will discuss our findings of the JCMT campaign of the interstellar comet and its implications compared with Solar-System comets.

presentations.presentation_title: Observations of the 3i Atlas Interstellar Object by SWI/JUICE Early Results
presentations.institution: Max Planck Institute for Solar System Research
presentations.abstract: The Submillimeter Wave Instrument (SWI) aboard the JUpiter Icy Moon Explorer (JUICE) conducted a series of targeted observations of the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS, discovered on July 1, 2025, by the ATLAS survey in Chile. As the third confirmed interstellar object to traverse our solar system—following 1I/ʻOumuamua and 2I/Borisov—3I/ATLAS offers a unique opportunity to study the composition and physical properties of material from outside the Solar System. JUICE executed dedicated observations of the comet between November 2 and November 19, 2025, during which the SWI instrument performed four 30-minute observations at a distance of approximately 80 million kilometers. The observations targeted the ground-state rotational transitions of ortho- and para-water in the 600 GHz and 1200 GHz frequency bands, using frequency-switching mode to maximize on-source integration time. We present the initial data reduction, calibration procedures, and first results from the SWI observations. These include derived rotational line intensities and preliminary constraints on the water production rate. We discuss the implications of the measurements in the context of interstellar comet composition, comparing them with other observations. The results provide early insights into the volatile content of an interstellar visitor and contribute to our understanding of the chemical diversity of cometary material across stellar systems.

presentations.presentation_title: Nitrogen Speciation in Chondritic Materials Revealed by Partial Fluorescence Yield N-XANES Spectroscopy
presentations.abstract: Carbonaceous chondrites contain a variety of organic compounds, including amino acids, dominated by insoluble organic matter (IOM). Although nitrogen-bearing compounds are far less abundant than carbon, they are of particular interest as potential precursors of prebiotic molecules. However, their chemical speciation remains poorly constrained owing to low concentrations and analytical limitations. In this study, we investigated nitrogen-containing organic matter in a variety of carbonaceous chondrites and xenolithic carbon-rich clasts using high-sensitivity partial fluorescence yield nitrogen K-edge X-ray absorption near-edge structure (PFY N-XANES) spectroscopy at SPring-8.Most samples exhibit three characteristic N-XANES peaks: (A) ~398.7 eV, assigned to imines/pyridinic N; (B) ~399.7 eV, attributed to pyridinic N/nitriles; and (C) ~400.8 eV, corresponding to amines/pyrrolic N and/or ammonium salts. Xenolithic clast from the Zag meteorite, as well as ungrouped type 2 chondrites including Tagish Lake and Tarda, show an intense peak C, indicating enrichment in non-conjugated nitrogen species. Such differences found in N-bearing compounds may reflect differences in the environments in which they formed or were altered during the early evolution of the Solar System. Both intact meteorites and IOM extracted from Orgueil (CI), Murchison (CM), and Tagish Lake (ungrouped C2) were analyzed. Comparisons between intact samples and IOM reveal pronounced differences in nitrogen speciation. In particular, peaks B and C are significantly diminished in IOM, indicating that acid-labile nitrogen-bearing moieties, such as amides and ammonium salts, as well as solvent-extractable N-compounds, are partially lost or altered during demineralization. These results imply that extraterrestrial nitrogen compounds are more diverse and abundant in pristine materials than previously inferred from IOM alone. This study demonstrates the effectiveness of PFY N-XANES spectroscopy for characterizing nitrogen chemistry in meteorites and provides new insights into the inventory and alteration of nitrogen-bearing organic matter relevant to prebiotic chemistry on early Earth.

presentations.presentation_title: Small-scale Chemical Heterogeneity in Ryugu, CI, and CY Chondrites: Insights Into CI-like Materials
presentations.abstract: The Hayabusa2 mission returned samples from the Cb-type asteroid Ryugu to Earth. Initial analysis revealed mineralogical, chemical, and isotopic similarities between Ryugu samples and CI chondrites. Consequently, the need for a comprehensive understanding of CI-like materials, including Ryugu, CI, and Yamato-type (CY) chondrites, has increased. CY chondrites are ungrouped carbonaceous chondrites with mineralogical and chemical characteristics similar to those of CI chondrites; however, the parent-body processes responsible for their similarities and differences remain unclear. Variations in elemental abundances reflect not only conditions prior to accretion, but also secondary parent-body processes such as aqueous alteration. In this study, we investigate small-scale chemical heterogeneity in Ryugu, CI, and CY chondrites using ~1 mg of material per measurement, allowing us to probe elemental distributions at fine scales relevant to their detailed evolutionary processes.We measured abundances of highly siderophile elements (HSE; Re, Os, Ir, Ru, Pt, Rh, Pd, and Au), volatile chalcophile elements (S, Ge, As, Se, and Te), as well as some major elements (Mg, Al, and Ca). Ryugu, CI, and CY samples give homogeneous relative abundances for most of these elements. Ryugu samples are enriched in Ca and Mn abundances, due to high abundances of carbonates. Y-980115 (CY) samples show Au depletion, possibly caused by heating events on the parent body. While Ryugu and CI samples do not show fractionation among HSEs, their absolute abundances vary substantially (0.5-1.1xCI). Following solar nebula condensation models, siderophile elements initially condensed into FeNi-alloy. Subsequent aqueous alteration destroyed these primary phases, redistributing HSEs into secondary minerals precipitated from the aqueous solution. Homogeneous relative HSE abundances may reflect the nature of the primary materials accreted as the building block of the parent bodies, while the variable absolute abundances are controlled by the variation in the abundance of secondary host phases residing in the 1 mg-size samples.

presentations.presentation_title: The Nature and Formation of Silica Minerals in Eucrite Meteorites: Insight Into the Protoplanetary Magma Crystallization
presentations.abstract: Silica polymorphs in achondrites provide key constraints on crystallization processes associated with thermal evolution in the early solar system. Eucrites, the largest group of achondrites, contains several silica polymorphs whose origins have remained debated [e.g., Ono et al., 2021, MAPS; Kanemaru et al., 2024, Sci. Rep.]. In this study, we conducted a systematic investigation of silica polymorphs in eucrites using cathodoluminescence imaging and laser Raman spectroscopy, enabling detailed characterization of their textural relationships and crystallization process. The analyzed eucrites exhibit significant variations in the proportions of tridymite, cristobalite, and quartz. Based on the dominant silica phase, we classify them into four distinct “Si-groups”: Si-0 (cristobalite-dominant), Si-I (quartz-dominant), Si-II (quartz + tridymite-dominant), and Si-III (tridymite-dominant) [Kanemaru et al., 2025, MAPS]. Our observations indicate that tridymite and cristobalite commonly occur as lath-shaped euhedral crystals, whereas quartz appears anhedral and is often associated with opaques and phosphates. These relationships suggest that silica polymorphs formed at different stages and through multiple pathways. We propose a new crystallization model in which tridymite forms from alkali-rich immiscible melts (≥ ~1060 °C), cristobalite from rapidly quenched melts (~1060 °C), and quartz from highly differentiated melts and/or by solid-state transformation of tridymite or cristobalite through interaction with sulfur-rich vapor below ~1025 °C. This framework explains the observed mineralogical diversity without invoking secondary heating or shock metamorphism. The results provide new constraints on magmatic differentiation and thermal processing on the HED parent body, offering broader implications for early protoplanetary crust formation.

presentations.presentation_title: Fluid Moblization of Rare Earth Elements and Their Isotopic Systems During Terrestrial Alteration
presentations.abstract: The Antarctic meteorite collection plays a pivotal role for cosmochemistry as the recovered fragments constitute by number more than 60% of the population of all meteorites collected to date. Meteorites accumulate due to the very slow movements of the glacial ice. Although Antarctic meteorite finds are typically better protected from terrestrial weathering by burial in the ice than meteorites collected from hot deserts, the exposure of Antarctic meteorites to the extreme Antarctic climate during an extended period of time can still lead to physical and chemical alteration. As such, previous studies examined the effect of Antarctic alteration not only using mobile elements but also relatively immobile elements, such as the rare earth elements (REEs). However, no systematic studies regarding the effects on REEs are available for chondrites and the detailed mechanisms of the alteration remain poorly understood. Therefore, we evaluated the effect of Antarctic alteration on REEs in H chondrites (HCs), particularly focusing on their Sm-Nd and Lu-Hf isotope systematics, and investigated the underlying alteration mechanism, using a comprehensive analysis combining bulk analysis with in-situ measurements. According to our results, the Sm-Nd and Lu-Hf isotopic compositions of the characterized HCs fall within the range measured for chondrite falls regardless of their degrees of weathering. However, a heavily altered Antarctic HC indicates various element losses including for the REEs, disturbing their Sm-Nd and Lu-Hf isotopic compositions. Based on distribution maps of trace elements obtained using LA-ICP-TOF-MS, such an elemental mobilization is interpreted to result from the partial dissolution of Ca-phosphates taking place when fluids pass through the meteorite interiors during terrestrial weathering. This study confirms the usefulness of Antarctic meteorites for some radiogenic age determinations. However, when the partial dissolution of Ca-phosphate phases by fluids during terrestrial weathering is extensive, both the elemental and isotopic compositions of the sample are modified.

presentations.presentation_title: An Experimental Study of Sodium and Potassium Volatile Behavior Under High Temperature and Controlled Atmosphere
presentations.institution: University of Sciences and Technology of Oran-Mohamed Boudiaf (USTO-MB)
presentations.abstract: Alkalis, mainly lithophile in terrestrial magmatic systems, tend to become volatile when submitted to high temperatures. Understanding their fractionation between solids, liquids and gases, in terrestrial or pre-terrestrial environments, would improve our knowledge on the earliest moments of the solar system evolution, as documented by chondrules and Calcium-Aluminum rich refractory inclusions (CAIs). Aiming to provide new insights into this matter and to participate into unraveling the phenomena behind the unexpectedly high alkali contents registered within these oldest known condensates of the primordial solar nebula, we attempted to constrain, experimentally, the general volatilization law of both Na and K elements, using a vertical Gero-type furnace. The experiments were carried out under a fixed run Temperature of 1511 °C and variable heating times, initial composition of the mixtures (deduced from the CaO-MgO-Al 2 O 3 -SiO 2 system), redox conditions and partial pressures of the gaseous species. The obtained results showed the strong dependence of the volatilization’s rate and speed on each of the aforementioned parameters; with a clear positive correlation between the latter, the reduction rate of the atmosphere, induced within the furnace, and the basicity index of the silicate liquids. The solubility of the considered alkalis was also enhanced for the liquids with the highest silica contents (i.e. acid ones). Finally, the volatilization (s.s.) seemed to be the rate limiting process. The re-condensation of the studied elements was the competing process and governed by the partial pressures of the evaporated gaseous species, present around the silicate liquids. However, even if it has been possible to constrain the relatively simple volatilization law of Na, the contamination rate was a relatively hampering factor that made this task more challenging for K, even if its overall similar behavior to that of Na would imply a similar outcome.

presentations.presentation_title: Late Fluid Flow in a Primitive Asteroid Revealed by Excess Hafnium-176 in Ryugu
presentations.abstract: Carbonaceous asteroids are the source of the most primitive meteorites and represent leftover planetesimals that formed from ice and dust in the outer Solar System and may have delivered volatiles to the terrestrial planets. Understanding the aqueous activity of asteroids is key to deciphering their thermal, chemical, and orbital evolution, with implications for the origin of water on the terrestrial planets. Analyses of the objects, in particular pristine samples returned from asteroid Ryugu, have provided detailed information on fluid–rock interactions within a few million years after parent body formation. However, the long-term fate of asteroidal water remains poorly understood. Here we show that Ryugu samples contain excess radiogenic hafnium-176 unsupported by the decay of co-existing lutetium-176. This excess is attributed to lutetium transport by alkali–phosphorous-rich fluids more than one billion years after formation. Such late fluid flow was probably triggered by an impact that generated heat for ice melting and opened rock fractures for fluid migration. This contrasts the early aqueous activity powered by short-lived radioactive decay, with limited fluid flow and little elemental fractionation. Our results imply that carbonaceous planetesimals accreted by the terrestrial planets could have retained not only hydrous minerals but also aqueous water, leading to an upward revision of the water inventory by a factor of 2 to 3.

presentations.presentation_title: Impact-delivered Iron and Magnetisation Enhancements in Impact Basins: the Case of Mercury
presentations.abstract: Crustal magnetic field signatures on Mercury coincide with some, but not all, of the mid-sized impact basins at northern latitudes investigated by the MESSENGER spacecraft. We investigate the extent to which iron-rich impactors can produce local iron enrichment in the crust, resulting in detectable magnetisation enhancements relative to the surrounding regions. We used the iSALE-2D shock-physics hydrocode to simulate the formation of mid-sized impact basins on Mercury, with a focus on the fate of the impactor. The impactor sizes were 10, 15, 20, and 25 km in diameter, with impact speeds appropriate for Mercury of 15, 25, 40, and 60 km/s, resulting in craters with rim diameters of 50 to 450 km on Mercury. Spherical impactors with three different compositions were considered: completely chondritic, completely iron and a 50-50 differentiated in radius between a pure iron core and chondritic mantle. Porosity effects are also included, motivated by telescopic observations of iron-rich asteroids. We report on the survivability of impactors and the depositional province of surviving impactors within impact basins.We calculate the rate of impactor survivability based on its iron content and size, and the impactor speed appropriate for dynamic conditions at Mercury, and compare our results with the observations of the iron-rich asteroid population.

presentations.presentation_title: Beyond A Point Source: Realistic Modelling Of The RIMFAX Ground Penetrating Radar At Jezero Crater
presentations.abstract: Planetary exploration increasingly focuses on the Martian and Lunar subsurfaces, to survey resources, water ice, and potential biosignatures. Ground Penetrating Radar (GPR) is a critical, non-destructive instrument for planetary subsurface exploration. The RIMFAX (Radar Imager for Mars' Subsurface Experiment) GPR antenna, aboard the NASA 2020 mission Perseverance rover, has generated approximately 40km of data since February 2021, mapping the complex sedimentary history of the Jezero crater subsurface. This crater preserves a clear paleolake and river delta system, making it a high priority site for locating potential biosignatures. However, interpreting this data is challenged by an absence of readily available, high-fidelity 3D numerical models of the RIMFAX antenna and its interaction with the rover structure. Approximating RIMFAX as a simple point-source, rather than a full 3D model, can cause deviations in the waveforms, as well as fail to model the electromagnetic coupling with the rover structure, leading to flawed interpretations of the subsurface.To address this problem, we present robust and geometrically accurate numerical models of the RIMFAX antenna and the Perseverance rover for use in gprMax, an open source finite-difference time domain (FDTD) solver. Our workflow adapts existing surface mesh models, voxelating them so that they are compatible in an FDTD environment. Material properties and excitation sources are derived from available technical specifications, or constrained through optimization processes, where proprietary data is unavailable. Validation of the models shows highly consistent results with both laboratory measurements and in-situ planetary data. These freely available models enable the community to produce more realistic radargrams, leading to more accurate characterisations of the mechanical and mineralogical properties of the Martian subsurface. Furthermore, this modelling workflow provides a scalable framework for future rover-mounted GPR systems across the solar system.

presentations.presentation_title: The Juno-Supporting Earth-Based Observing Campaign
presentations.institution: Jet Propulsion Laboratory, California Institute of Technology
presentations.abstract: To provide important spatial, spectral and temporal context to measurements made by the spacecraft, the science team coordinates an international network of Earth-based observations. This network’s measurements cover a broad spectral range with over 60 groups contributing to the campaign. These observations constitute specific enhancements to Juno’s own data. (1) They provide knowledge about the evolution of features detected by the spacecraft at a single point in time. (2) Contextual information is gathered about the larger spatial environment surrounding the limited regions covered by Juno. (3) The spectral range covered by Juno’s suite of instruments is expanded to cover X-ray through radio wavelengths. (4) Supporting measurements also assess the extent to which distant phenomena within the Jovian system may influence atmospheric or auroral properties detected by Juno’s instruments, such as the mass loading from Io by tracking its observed volcanic activity and the opacity of its torus. The ultimate goal of these measurements is to relate properties of the deep atmosphere, the focus of Juno’s mission, to the state of the “weather layer” at much lower pressures Of special consideration during Juno’s emission extensions are observations of thermal emission that cover narrow atmospheric regions where temperature profiles are created from the phase change of the high-beam antenna’s radio signal as it is being occulted by Jupiter’s atmosphere. The spectral region and timeline of all of these observations are summarized in the web site: https://www.missionjuno.swri.edu/planned-observations. Besides professional astronomers, the Juno mission also benefits significantly from a network of dedicated amateur astronomers who provided a quasi-continuous picture of the evolution of features observed by Juno’s instruments.

presentations.presentation_title: Effects of Stable Layers on Atmospheric Dynamics in Giant Planet Atmospheres
presentations.abstract: Stable layers in giant planets are not well understood, and their interactions with the atmosphere remain largely uncharacterized. However, these layers are crucial for understanding the mixing between planetary interiors and atmospheres, as well as heat transport processes. Models suggest their importance in the evolutionary pathways of both the interiors and atmospheres of these planets. This study investigates the effects of stable layers on atmospheric dynamics through gravitational implications on Jupiter and a convection-driven general circulation model. Our experiments demonstrate that the position, extent, and stratification factor of stable layers are vital for their effectiveness in dissipating atmospheric flows and their detectability in gravity data. Additionally, we show that the evolution of these layers is significant: integrating them into existing jet structures or initiating jets from the onset of convection under their influence leads to divergent outcomes. These results highlight the complex relationship between stable layers and atmospheric dynamics, providing new insights into how these layers influence the behavior of giant planets and enhancing our understanding of their climate system.

presentations.presentation_title: Gas Giants as Laboratories for Planet Formation and Atmospheric Characterization
presentations.abstract: The population of extrasolar gas giants, which range from close-in orbits to regions beyond the snow line, provides a unique testbed for studying the fundamental processes of planet formation, such as orbital migration driven by planet-disk interactions and gravitational perturbations. Since the launch of the James Webb Space Telescope, transit spectroscopy of close-in gas giants has also been revealing their atmospheric properties, including chemical compositions and the formation of cloud and haze. Detailed atmospheric characterization of gas giants allows us to probe their birthplaces and formation environments. Recently, high-resolution observations of dust continuum and H alpha emission in the PDS 70 system provide compelling evidence of ongoing mass accretion onto forming gas giants and their circumplanetary disks, which serve as sites of satellite formation. These observational breakthroughs are transforming our understanding of the formation and evolution of gas giants in the solar system and beyond. In this talk, we present recent observations of extrasolar gas giants and theoretical advances in formation and evolutionary pathways of gas giants.

presentations.presentation_title: An Overview of the Juno Radio Occultations at Jupiter
presentations.abstract: Radio occultation experiments provide one of the most direct probes of the shallow atmosphere of Jupiter, the only region of the gas giant accessible to in-situ measurements and a key interface between the deep interior and the observable cloud layer. By measuring the refraction of radio signals as they pass through the atmosphere, radio occultations yield high-vertical-resolution profiles of temperature, pressure, and composition, offering unique constraints on the thermal and dynamical structure of the stratosphere and upper troposphere. During its extended mission, beginning in July 2023, the Juno spacecraft has conducted the first radio occultations of Jupiter since the Voyager era, significantly expanding both the spatial coverage and scientific scope of these measurements. Using coherent two-way, multi-frequency radio links and detailed ray-tracing techniques, Juno’s occultations provide precise vertical profiles up to pressures of ~0.5 bar across a wide range of latitudes. When combined with contemporary ground-based observations, these profiles place new constraints on the variability and circulation of Jupiter’s shallow atmosphere. In this talk, I will present an overview of results from two years of Juno radio occultations, highlighting what they reveal about Jupiter’s stratospheric and upper-tropospheric structure and how they compare with earlier infrared measurements from Voyager and Cassini, as well as modern ground-based datasets. Particular attention will be given to recent occultations sampling Jupiter’s polar regions, which offer new insights into the thermal structure and dynamics of the polar stratospheric vortex. These measurements also give us the ability to better measure the shape and size of the planet. We show that at the equator the planet is 14 km smaller than previously thought. Together, these observations illustrate the renewed power of radio occultations as a tool for understanding Jupiter’s atmospheric dynamics and its coupling across vertical and latitudinal scales.

presentations.presentation_title: Physical Properties of the Surface of Enceladus at the Global Scale Based on New Super-resolution Map of the Cassini-vims Data
presentations.institution: Institut de Physique du Globe de Paris (IPGP)
presentations.abstract: Saturn’s moon Enceladus has emerged as a key target for planetary exploration and has been prioritized for future dedicated missions, due to its diverse geomorphology coupled with numerous discoveries by the Cassini-Huygens mission hinting to possible habitable conditions (geothermal activity, subsurface ocean, abundance of volatiles). Cassini’s Visual and Infrared Mapping Spectrometer (VIMS) observations of Enceladus have revealed a surface spectrally dominated by water ice, with variations primarily attributed to differences in grain size, temperature, and crystallinity (Brown et al., 2006). This work presents a global study of these physical properties of the surface of Enceladus leveraging the new VIMS super-resolution map by Ntinos et al. (2025). To achieve this we explore a variety of analytical spectroscopic tools available, namely the Shkuratov radiative transfer model (Shkuratov et al., 1999; Poulet et al., 2002; Khuller and Emran 2025), empirical spectral indicators such as band depths, band ratios, and continuum slopes (Jaumann et al., 2008; Taffin et al., 2012; Scipioni et al., 2017) and laboratory measurements of water-ice spectra (Stephan et al., 2021). Combined with the results from the inversion of the Hapke radiative transfer model by Cruz-Mermy et al. (2025), this analysis provides a consolidated spectral analysis of the VIMS global hyperspectral map of Enceladus at an unprecedented spatial resolution. By correlating these physical properties with their geomorphological context (Crow and Pappalardo, 2015; Kinczyk et al., 2024) and plume particle deposition models (Kempf et al., 2010; Southworth et al., 2019) we offer new insights into the processes shaping the surface of Enceladus tied to its internal structure and evolution.

presentations.presentation_title: Reassessing Cryovolcanic Targets on Ganymede in Advance of JUICE
presentations.abstract: Cryovolcanism is a potentially important process in shaping Ganymede’s surface and may provide insights into the moon’s internal evolution and habitability potential. ESA’s JUpiter ICy moons Explorer (JUICE), launched in 2023, will deliver the first dedicated, high-resolution investigation of Ganymede’s surface and interior. In advance of JUICE’s arrival in the Jovian system, it is timely to reassess previously proposed cryovolcanic regions using a consistent and comparative framework. Based on Voyager and Galileo observations, approximately 20 paterae and other morphologically distinctive features have been proposed as candidate cryovolcanic regions. However, their geological context and compositional variability have not yet been evaluated in a systematic and comparative manner. Here, we present a reanalysis of all proposed candidate regions, combining regional geomorphological assessment with comparative near-infrared spectral analysis. Reprocessed Galileo Near-Infrared Mapping Spectrometer (NIMS) data are examined using a uniform linear spectral unmixing approach, with emphasis on relative spectral trends and temperature-dependent behavior rather than absolute compositional determinations. This approach allows for direct comparison across regions observed under varying conditions. Our analysis reveals distinct spectral groupings among candidate regions, ranging from ice-dominated terrains to areas exhibiting enhanced non-ice spectral components. When considered together with morphological characteristics, these groupings suggest that multiple formation and modification processes may be represented, including end-member cases consistent with cryovolcanic resurfacing and/or brine-related processes. Rather than providing definitive geological interpretations, this work establishes a pre-JUICE baseline for target prioritization and observation planning. We discuss implications for future high-resolution imaging and spectroscopy by the JANUS and MAJIS instruments, and outline how forthcoming JUICE observations can discriminate between competing geological scenarios.

presentations.presentation_title: A Novel Solid-Phase Extraction Technology for Kerogen Using Ionic Liquids
presentations.abstract: Kerogen, the insoluble organic fraction in sedimentary rocks, has been reported not only on Earth but also on Mars, highlighting its importance for planetary organic geochemistry and astrobiology. Unlike bitumen, which is readily extractable using organic solvents, kerogen-bound organic compounds are difficult to access due to their insoluble nature. In this study, we investigate a novel solid-phase extraction approach using ionic liquids to recover saturated hydrocarbons from kerogen. Four geological samples ranging in age from the Paleozoic to the Cenozoic were examined. After remove bitumen, the residual kerogen was treated with four types of ionic liquids (N₄OH, IMD, TPO₄, TSO₄ + EDA) in combination with organic solvents. The mixtures were stirred overnight, and the recovered organic phases were analyzed by GC–MS. Compared to solvent-only controls, samples treated with ionic liquids—particularly IMD—showed enhanced extraction efficiencies, with saturated hydrocarbon signals increasing by several-fold to several hundred-fold. Additional microwave-assisted heating of the kerogen–ionic liquid residue prior to re-extraction further enhanced hydrocarbon recovery in some samples. Notably, extracted compounds include saturated hydrocarbon biomarkers such as pristane and phytane. These results demonstrate that ionic-liquid-assisted extraction can effectively liberate kerogen-bound organic molecules, suggesting potential applications for detecting biomarker compounds in Martian kerogen and advancing astrobiological exploration of planetary surfaces.

presentations.presentation_title: Investigating the Role of Thermal Erosion in the Formation of Putative Cryovolcanic Features on Ariel and Triton
presentations.abstract: Terrestrial volcanism is an important process that can shape planetary surfaces through the generation of features such as lava flows, volcanic constructs, and even channels (lava rilles/tubes). Cryovolcanism (icy volcanism where water acts as ‘lava’) could be a similarly important process shaping the surfaces of icy bodies. Thermal erosion, where an effusive lava flow erodes a preexisting surface, can form negative topographic volcanic features such as channels in terrestrial settings. Thermal erosion could similarly form negative topographic features on icy surfaces. Putative cryovolcanic features are identified on many outer solar system bodies, including both Neptune’s moon Triton and Uranus’ moon Ariel. Here, we investigate the role of thermal erosion in the formation of putative negative topographic cryovolcanic features on both Triton (pits) and Ariel (chasmata). We use the GIS mapping software JMARS to analyze features of interest by first measuring for their lengths, widths, and depths. We determine that on average, Triton’s pits are ~300–400 m in depth and Ariel’s chasmata are ~1300–1500 m in depth. The measured depths for Triton’s pits appear to be within the range of most terrestrial rilles (10s to 100s of m in depth). However, Ariel’s chasmata are deeper than most terrestrial rilles, suggesting that thermal erosion may not be the sole geologic process in their formation (i.e. extensional fractures create initial fractures that are later deepened through thermal erosion), or a different formation process occurred (i.e. spreading centers). We will incorporate the results of our geologic measurements into a future thermal erosion model to determine the extent to which a cryoflow can erode an icy surface.

presentations.presentation_title: Mud and Lakes at Low Latitudes on Titan
presentations.institution: Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory
presentations.abstract: Titan's low latitudes host vast fields of sand dunes like Earth's deserts, but like our desert regions, there are occasional rainstorms that produce transient rivers and lakes. Furthermore, the presence of surface moisture can create damp sand and mud that may require consideration for sample acquisition or mobility systems on space missions. I review the likelihood, seasonal and location dependence of such dampness, noting the association of low-latitude rainfall with the equinox season (during which Cassini observed ground-darkening attributed to moisture after a rainstorm) and the in-situ detection by the Huygens probe of surface moisture in what seems to be a fluvially-modified region. Cassini infrared observations detected a dark patch which, while it lacks obvious large-scale liquid textures in radar imaging, was found to be in a local depression and so may be prone to transient refilling by rainfall even if it dries out for much of the year. I review these considerations also for the Dragonfly landing and operations area near Selk crater.

presentations.presentation_title: Interdunes of Titan: Dragonfly Landing Site and Earth Analogs
presentations.abstract: The dune regions of Saturn’s moon Titan cover up to 20% of the body, with at least half the area being interdunes, or the space between the dunes. Interdunes are representative of the preexisting geology, and therefore tend to be older and more varied than the dunes. As the NASA Dragonfly rotorcraft will land on interdunes in the Shangri La sand sea, it is of great importance to better understand the properties and variety of interdunes possible on Titan. We compare three Earth analog settings: Oak City of central Utah, the United Arab Emirates and the northern Namib sand sea, with others to follow. The Oak City interdunes are characterized by Lake Bonneville lakebed clays, last covered by water at 10 ka, though they can become flooded and reworked in the modern age. The United Arab Emirates interdunes can be liquid rich, while others have carbonate or evaporite cobbles or crusts on a clay substrate. These were dated using Optically Stimulated Luminescence (OSL) techniques to be 9 ka at 1 m depth, while dunes were modern. Interdunes in the northern Namib Sand Sea have fluvially-derived, rounded, translucent quartz cobbles up to 6 cm, underlain by clay. Interdunes are generally flat, though fluvial processes have led to elevation changes across the Namib interdunes of several to tens of meters as determined by drone imaging. The OSL age for a 1 m depth interdune was 44 ka, with dunes being modern. The contrast in age between dunes and interdunes shows that non-aeolian materials and processes are dominant at interdunes, such as groundwater and fluvial action. Cryovolcanic and impact materials, targets for Dragonfly, might also be exposed at Titan’s interdune surfaces. Further studies on the compositional, textural and elevational differences possible across Earth’s interdunes will better prepare us for Dragonfly.

presentations.presentation_title: Phosphorus and Metal Accumulation within Cold Alkaline Lakes: Implications for Salts in Planetesimals and Phosphate on Early Mars
presentations.abstract: Water-rock interactions at low temperatures are becoming increasingly important for understanding aqueous environments and habitability on Solar system bodies. Geological evidence has been found of cold lacustrine environments on early Mars and of the freezing of liquid water on icy planetesimals. Here, we focus on alkaline-saline lakes in Mongolia as analogues for such low-temperature aqueous environments. Those lakes freeze during the cold season, partitioning the lake water from the atmosphere. We conducted field surveys and a geochemical model of elemental behaviors in the lakes during freezing.Our field surveys show that removal of water by freezing results in accumulations of most dissolved materials, including dissolved carbonate species, in lake water. On the other hand, accumulations of specific species are limited, such as calcium, arsenate, and phosphate. The pH of lake water decreased after freezing. These behaviors can be explained by our geochemical model, considering freezing, salt precipitation, and adsorption onto lake-floor sediments. Our model shows that accumulations of dissolved carbonate cause precipitation of thermodynamically metastable carbonate salts, buffering concentrations of cations, such as calcium. In addition, accumulations of dissolved carbonate can decrease the pH of lake water. The pH decrease could promote the adsorption of arsenate and phosphate onto sedimentary iron oxide particles and suppress their accumulation. The suppression of phosphate accumulation, in turn, would prevent the precipitation of phosphate salts.Phosphate and carbonate salts have been observed in samples returned from the asteroid Ryugu, precipitated from porewater in planetesimals. On Mars, iron-bearing phosphate was recently found in paleo-lake sediments containing iron oxides on Mars. Based on our surveys and model, we discuss the formation conditions of such salts in icy planetesimals and the availability of phosphate in lake water on early Mars.

presentations.presentation_title: Solving HCN Availability on an Oxidative Early Earth by Mineral-facilitated Amino Acid Degradation.
presentations.abstract: Hydrogen cyanide (HCN) is central to prebiotic synthesis of amino acids, peptides, nucleobases, and lipid-like compounds. However, growing geochemical and isotopic evidence suggests that early Earth may have been dominated by an oxidizing atmosphere, under which traditional HCN formation pathways based on methane and ammonia become inefficient. This creates a challenge between the necessity of HCN in prebiotic chemistry and its limited availability from atmospheric processes.In biology, HCN is synthesized from amino acids. Meanwhile, amino acids can form under oxidizing conditions from CO 2 , being available on an oxidizing prebiotic Earth. Therefore, we hypothesize that amino acids could have served as precursors for HCN generation.Here we experimentally demonstrated prebiotic pathway for HCN formation by the aqueous oxidation of amino acids by minerals under anoxic conditions. Screening 38 minerals reveals manganese dioxide (MnO 2 ) as particularly effective, producing up to 0.90 ± 0.02 mM HCN from glycine within 24 h. Isotopic labeling confirms that HCN originates from the 2-carbon of glycine, while ICP-OES identifies MnO 2 as the electron acceptor, reduced to Mn(OH) 2 . HCN formation proceeds over a broad pH (2–12.6) and temperature (6–60 °C) range, with enhanced yields at low temperatures, reaching 1.72 ± 0.07 mM at 6 °C. Ammonia and formate are produced, and oxidation of other amino acids yields their corresponding keto acids, indicating oxidative deamination with α-proton abstraction as the rate-determining step, supported by a pronounced kinetic isotope effect.These results demonstrate that HCN can arise prebiotically from amino acids under oxidizing geochemical conditions. In this framework, amino acids plays as precursors of HCN and as sources of central metabolic intermediates. The coupled generation of HCN and keto acids links mineral-driven chemistry to both prebiotic synthesis and protometabolic pathways, offering a geochemically plausible bridge between prebiotic chemistry and early biochemistry in oxidizing planetary environments.

presentations.presentation_title: Mineralogy and Wavelength-dependent Photoresponse of Chiral Molecules on Simulated Asteroidal Surfaces
presentations.abstract: The emergence of chiral asymmetry, a fundamental prerequisite for life as we know it, is a central question in astrobiology. Asteroids are considered key delivery vehicles of prebiotic organic molecules to the early Earth, but the preservation and chiral integrity of these compounds on asteroidal surfaces are subject to complex photochemical processes influenced by solar ultraviolet (UV) radiation and the local mineralogical environment. This study investigates the stability and potential for chiral selection of amino acids (alanine, glutamic acid, tyrosine) and glucose when exposed to UVB and UVC radiation in the presence of two distinct asteroid regolith simulants, a mafic mineral-rich type (JMSS-1) and an aqueous alteration mineral-rich type (CHG). Our results demonstrate that organic preservation is governed by a wavelength-dependent interplay with mineralogy. Mafic minerals provided significant protection against UVC but catalyzed decomposition under UVB, whereas aqueous minerals promoted pervasive photodegradation under UVC. Critically, chiral selection was found to show molecule-specific, but concomitantly sporadic effects. Observations of UV-induced racemization further indicate that radiation can actively erode, rather than establish, enantiomeric excesses. These findings collectively suggest that UV photochemistry alone is an unlikely primary driver for establishing homochirality, with the local mineralogy playing a complementary and crucial role in determining the chiral signature of any preserved organics. This work provides an essential experimental framework for interpreting data on chiral organic molecules from ongoing and future asteroid missions, highlighting the necessity of contextual mineralogical analysis.

presentations.presentation_title: A Terrestrial Analog for Martian Hematite Spherules from Serpentinite Soil-derived Iron Nodules in Sri Lanka
presentations.abstract: Martian hematite spherules are widely interpreted as evidence of aqueous iron mineralization, necessitating well-characterized terrestrial analogs to constrain their formation. We present iron-rich nodules from serpentinite-derived lateritic soils at Ussangoda and Ginigalpelessa in southern Sri Lanka as a promising analog system. These nodules occur as isolated spheroids and clustered crusts in surficial lateritic horizons, ranging from a few millimeters to ~1.5 cm in diameter and locally incorporating detrital fragments. Petrography reveals concentric banding, consistent with incremental accretion. XRD mineralogy identifies hematite and goethite as dominant phases with subordinate magnetite, indicating fluctuating redox conditions. Bulk geochemistry illustrates strong Fe enrichment (TFe 2 O 3 ~48-62 wt%), elevated MnO (~1.1-1.3 wt%), substantial volatiles (LOI ~10 wt%), and strong depletion of Mg-Ca-alkalis, consistent with advanced lateritic weathering of an ultramafic protolith. High Cr-Ni-Co abundances preserve the ultramafic signature, whereas variable Si-Al contents reflect admixed silicate detritus and quartz-rich nuclei. We interpret these as pedogenic Fe‑oxide/oxyhydroxide concretions formed by seasonal mobilization and redox‑controlled precipitation of iron via dissolution-reprecipitation around detrital nuclei. These Fe‑rich, concentrically banded concretions provide a natural laboratory to test how serpentinization/carbonation‑influenced pore‑water chemistry, episodic water flow, and redox fronts can generate hematite-goethite assemblages and spherical morphologies comparable to Martian hematite spherules. Thus, the Ussangoda system offers a critical terrestrial analog to refine rover‑scale criteria for interpreting aqueous iron mineralization and associated habitability‑relevant paleoenvironments on Mars.

presentations.presentation_title: Extreme Perchlorate Resistance in an Aspergillus Fungus from the Qaidam Basin
presentations.institution: Institute of Geology and Geophysics, Chinese Academy of Sciences
presentations.abstract: Subsurface water-ice on Mars is considered a potential habitable niche, where high concentrations of perchlorate salts can stabilize liquid water at temperatures as low as 180-198 K. Although perchlorates extend the window for water, they concurrently impose damaging osmotic, oxidative, and chaotropic stresses that threaten cellular integrity by degrading macromolecules (e.g., DNA and proteins). While some extremophiles exhibit notable perchlorate resistance even up to 2.2 M NaClO 4 , mechanistic insights into genomic and molecular adaptations remain limited. In this study, we isolated 16 fungal strains from Dalangtan Playa in the Qaidam Basin and assessed their extremotolerance. Among these strains, Aspergillus versicolor strain QDF06 demonstrated an exceptional capacity to grow in media containing up to 2.4 M NaClO 4 , representing the highest fungal perchlorate tolerance reported to date. Through morphological, genomic, and transcriptomic analyses, we identified key adaptive strategies of QDF06 that may support survival under Mars-relevant perchlorate-rich conditions. These findings expand the known boundaries of eukaryotic extremotolerance and provide a framework for evaluating the potential for life in highly oxidizing and chaotropic environments analogous to the subsurface of Mars.
presentations.session_title: Frontiers in Astrobiology: From Prebiotic Earth to Extraterrestrial Biosignatures

presentations.presentation_title: Thermal and Mechanical Signatures of Centimetre-scale Lunar Impacts from Observations and Numerical Impact Modelling
presentations.abstract: Analysis of impact flash observations provides constraints on lunar soil behaviour under hypervelocity conditions. Approximately 85% of peak flash temperatures lie between 2000 and 4500 K, consistent with the incipient vaporisation threshold for typical lunar soils. In the population of lunar impact flashes observed by ground-based telescopes, more than 75% of detected impactors fall within the mass range of 1–200 g (radii of ~0.5–3 cm), forming craters up to approximately 3.5 m in diameter (according to established scaling laws) [NELIOTA network]. Here, we investigate the relationship between cm-sized meteoroid impacts, observed impact flashes, and the physical properties of the lunar regolith to advance our understanding of the lunar near-surface. We use the iSALE shock-physics code to simulate the P-T-t history of impact-generated thermal and mechanical signatures in the uppermost crust of the Moon. We incorporate a range of regolith structures—specifically exponential porosity gradients and stratified layers—motivated by lunar remote sensing and geophysical surveys. These enhancements enable more accurate modelling of shock propagation, crater formation, and thermal emission in highly porous lunar crust. Together, these efforts advance our ability to interpret lunar impact flash data, improve meteoroid environment models, better constrain meteoroid impacts on the Moon as seismic sources, and deepen our understanding of the Moon’s dynamic near-surface processes.

presentations.presentation_title: Progress in the Development of the Ce‑7 Lunar Seismograph
presentations.institution: National Space Science Center, Chinese Academy of Sciences
presentations.abstract: After 50 years of the shutdown of Apollo seismographs in 1976, Chang’e-7 mission will deploy the first seismograph on the south pole of the Moon this year. We will present some details of the development of Chang’e-7 lunar seismograph. The development process followed a rigorous validation roadmap. Initial phases focused on principle verification and proof-of-concept prototypes to establish the feasibility of the detection mechanisms. This was followed by extensive electrical performance verification, ensuring tested the instrument's electrical functionality and key performance specifications, the engineering team executed a strict qualification testing campaign (Qualification Model phase) to validate the instrument’s structural and thermal resilience against the harsh space environment. Currently, the development has culminated in the production of the flight model. The instrument has successfully completed all system-level joint tests and final experimental verifications, demonstrating full compatibility with the spacecraft and mission requirements. The data confirms that all performance indicators meet or exceed the design specifications. We will also discuss the technical challenges overcome during the transition from the qualification phase to the flight model, as well as the expected performance during the mission operations.

presentations.presentation_title: In-situ Seismic Investigations of Asteroid Apophis with the Ramses Mission
presentations.abstract: The close flyby of asteroid (99942) Apophis in 2029 provides a unique opportunity to perform the first in-situ seismic investigation of an asteroid. The Seismic Instrument for Asteroids (SIA), to be deployed on the surface of Apophis by the RAMSES mission via a CubeSat platform, will measure seismic activity generated by tidal forces from Earth. SIA’s primary objective is to perform the first seismic measurements directly on the surface of an asteroid. The instrument will constrain surface mechanical properties during landing, characterize the ambient seismic noise, quantify the tidally induced seismicity, and probe the subsurface and internal structure of Apophis. These measurements are critical for planetary defense - improving impact risk assessment and mitigation strategies - and for understanding asteroid formation and evolution. SIA is a compact seismometer integrating three geophones with custom-built low-noise electronics. It is designed to achieve a noise level below 1.0 × 10⁻⁹ m/s/√Hz over the 5 - 200 Hz band. SIA will be deployed to the surface of Apophis prior to the asteroid’s closest approach to Earth with the goal of performing continuous monitoring around the perigee, when tidally induced seismicity is expected to peak. Additional observations prior to and after the Earth encounter will track the evolution of the asteroid’s seismicity and support background noise characterization. In this presentation we will introduce SIA and the RAMSES mission before presenting the details of the instrument and the planned operations. The RAMSES mission is a joint ESA-JAXA mission planned for launch in March 2028. RAMSES will reach asteroid Apophis in February 2029 before the asteroid’s flyby of the Earth on the 13th April 2029. SIA is being developed at ISAE-SUPAERO with support from the French Space Agency (CNES), in collaboration with IPGP.
