presentations.presentation_title: Seismic Coda Envelope as a Distance Proxy for Lunar Impact Localization
presentations.institution: Institut de Physique du Globe de Paris - Université Paris Cité
presentations.abstract: Meteoroid impacts are a prominent class of lunar seismic sources in the Apollo record. Due to the strong scattering and low attenuation in the lunar crust, these hypervelocity near-surface sources generate waveforms dominated by long codas, producing emergent onsets that obscure body wave phases. Consequently, classical source location based on travel times from confident P and S picking is feasible for only tens of large-magnitude events. In contrast, additional information can be extracted from the characteristic coda shape. Oberst (1989) proposed an empirical method to locate impacts using the distance dependence of coda peak amplitude and rise time, successfully locating 73 events. However, it suffers from limitations including algorithm ill-conditioning, simplified modeling assumptions, and weak sensitivity to distance within ~2000 km.In this study, we optimized and reformulated the two empirical coda–distance relations by incorporating seismic quanta scattering theory for the distance range up to 1200km. This enables the location of local lunar impacts that are commonly recorded by fewer than three stations and therefore cannot be located using classical travel-time methods. We first validated the method using impacts previously located by P- and S-wave travel times, by artificially limiting the number of stations to one or two. In both cases, the estimated locations agreed with reference solutions within ~200 km and exhibited strong robustness against noise. We then applied the approach to previously non-located impacts in the Apollo catalog. A total of 95 high-amplitude local events with identifiable coda envelope signatures were selected and located on an event-by-event basis using available station observations. The inferred locations are independently cross-validated through the distance dependence of coda shape.This coda-envelope–based approach provides a practical framework for locating lunar impacts under sparse station configurations and enrich the event catalog for future lunar interior and impact seismicity investigations.

presentations.presentation_title: Orbital Modulation of Seismicity in Titan’s Ice Shell
presentations.institution: Université Paris Cité, Institut de Physique du Globe de Paris, CNRS, France
presentations.abstract: NASA’s mission Dragonfly, the 4th mission of the New Frontiers Program, will explore Titan’s surface and subsurface environment in the mid-2030s in search of prebiotic chemistry. Among its payloads, the DraGMet geophysical package will include a short-period seismometer, offering a unique opportunity to probe Titan’s internal structure and active processes. Titan displays a wide range of surface features, including mountain chains, dune fields, and methane rivers and lakes, suggesting ongoing tectonic and geodynamic activity, where tidal force may play an important role. In this study, we investigate the potential for tidally driven seismicity on Titan and its modulation over the satellite’s orbital cycle. Using theoretically computed global tidal stress fields for a given internal structure, we evaluate fault reactivation through the Coulomb failure criterion and derive time-dependent rupture depths and stress drops at selected locations. These results are combined with a viscoelastic strain-rate formulation to estimate the cumulative seismic moment release over an orbital cycle. We then generate synthetic catalogs with magnitude constrained by observed fault lengths, allowing us to quantify variations in event rates and magnitudes as a function of orbital position. Our results predict a strong orbital modulation of seismic activity, with distinct periods of enhanced activity and periods of low activity. We further show that both the amplitude and timing of seismic activity are sensitive to Titan’s internal structure and frictional properties, leading to measurable shifts in seismicity patterns and optimal observation windows. These findings offer testable predictions for future seismic observations by Dragonfly.

presentations.presentation_title: South Pole Seismic Station (SPSS): an Active and Passive Seismic Deployment for Artemis Iv Astronauts Coupled with an Earth Ground Impact Flashes Telescopes Network
presentations.institution: Université Paris Cité, Institut de physique du globe de Paris, CNRS
presentations.abstract: The South Pole Seismic Station will be the 4 th seismometer deployed in the South hemisphere of the Moon after ChangE’7 (2026), FSS (2028) and LEMS on the Artemis 3 mission. This will be the second equipped with a spare unit of the InSight seismometer, a Very Broad Band vertical seismometer (VBBZ) with a sensitivity more than 10 times better than Apollo or LEMS at 1 Hz. Furthermore, the instrument will be deployed by the Artemis IV astronauts for ideal seismic coupling and leveling, minimizing the tilt and sun-related noise. SPSS will also be equipped with geophones, enabling to record an active seismic survey performed by the astronauts with a compact Portable Active Seismic Source (PASS) and to complement the VBBZ recording. SPSS will continue operating as a long-term seismic station after the astronauts leave. SPSS has the following four major science objectives: 1. Determine lunar interior structure to better understand the geologic processes that affect planetary bodies; 2. Understand the current lunar bombardment rate; 3. Monitor real-time environment affecting operations for astronauts and potential for future stable astrophysical and physics observatories; and 4. Determine near-surface and regolith properties to address active surface processes and polar volatiles. Objectives 1 and 2 will be completed by a worldwide network of Infra-red telescopes. This will allow to time and locate impacts occurring on the near side of the Moon, which will give a direct access to the absolute travel times of P and S waves for known epicentral distances when associated seismograms are recorded on the SPSS seismometer. This will complement the PASS active seismic experiment with several naturally provided explosive seismic profiles, enabling an unprecedent seismic imaging of the lunar subsurface and crust.

presentations.presentation_title: Scaling of Lunar and Martian Impact Seismic Sources with Impactor Properties
presentations.abstract: Meteorite impacts have been a major source of seismic signal during the Apollo missions, with almost 2000 detections. The InSight mission recorded nine impacts seismically, which were simultaneously imaged from orbit. Seismometers deployed by the future Chang’e 7, FSS and Artemis III-IV missions will capture signals from craters forming in the vicinity of their landing site — i.e., near the south pole of the Moon for CH7 and Artemis III-IV—and much further away. Some of them will be located, timed and characterized through Lunar Impact Flashes detections performed by earth-based telescopes observation of the near-side and high-resolution orbiter imaging, allowing to interpret their seismic signals with unprecedented levels of detail. In this project, we focus on the seismic generation process—how the properties of the impactor and the impacted material influence the recorded signals, and what these signals reveal about the impacted material itself. We have recently identified a scaling relationship between the corner frequency of the seismic signal, the kinetic energy of the impactor and the seismic properties of the impacted material. This relationship appears consistent across Apollo-era impacts, Martian impacts, and synthetic signals produced by high-fidelity hydrocode impact modeling. This suggests that the spectral properties of impact seismic signals are linked to the elastic properties of the impacted surface. Still, this relationship suffers from large uncertainties. In the present work, we address them by: 1) harmonizing existing measurements of corner frequencies and impactor momentum for both the Moon and Mars. 2) conducting a parametric study of the spectral characteristics of impact seismic signals through numerical simulations using impact hydrocodes. By combining numerical investigation with improved data analysis, we gain comprehension of how the spectral content of impact seismic signal varies with target material properties.

presentations.presentation_title: The results of the LIFs Geminids Campaign Taiwan (LGCT)
presentations.abstract: Lunar impact flashes (LIFs) are transient optical phenomena produced when meteoroids, typically centimeter- to decimeter-sized, impact the lunar surface at hypervelocity. A small fraction of the impact energy is converted into a short-lived optical flash detectable by ground-based telescopes equipped with sensitive video cameras. Observations of LIFs provide valuable constraints on meteoroid fluxes and impact processes in the Earth–Moon system. The Lunar Geminid Collaboration in Taiwan (LGCT) project aims to coordinate observational facilities in Taiwan and to collaborate with international Earth-based observing teams to monitor lunar impact flashes during the peak activity of the Geminid meteoroid stream, between 12 and 14 December 2025. The primary objective is to train amateur astronomers in standardized LIF observation and data-reduction techniques, thereby establishing a reliable and sustainable observer network. This effort serves as a preparatory step toward future citizen science programmes supporting CNSA’s Chang’e-7 mission (launch in 2026) and ESA’s LUMIO CubeSat mission (launch in 2028). During the campaign, more than thirty candidate impact flash events were identified, among which seven were simultaneously detected by at least two independent telescopes, all occurring on 14 December 2025. The physical properties of these impacts, including estimates of meteoroid sizes, masses, and resulting crater dimensions, are presented in this meeting.

presentations.presentation_title: Deep Auroral Ionization and High-energy Electron Precipitation in Jupiter’s North Polar Region from Juno MWR
presentations.abstract: During Juno’s extended mission, the spacecraft’s periapsis migrated toward Jupiter’s north pole, enabling high-resolution observations of auroral regions. At microwave wavelengths, these auroral features appear as localized reductions in brightness temperature (“cold spots”). Here we present observations from Juno Perijoves 56–72 using the Microwave Radiometer (MWR). MWR measures thermal emission from Jupiter’s deep atmosphere, which is partially absorbed by ionization produced by precipitating energetic electrons in the ionosphere. By exploiting MWR’s multi-frequency observations, we use the frequency dependence of electron–neutral collisional absorption to probe the vertical extent of auroral ionization at depths well below those accessible to ultraviolet measurements.We find systematic differences among auroral regions. The deepest ionization occurs at the Io footprint, is moderate along the main auroral oval, and is shallowest in the polar cap. Modeling of the multi-frequency absorption indicates that the Io footprint requires a substantial population of precipitating electrons with energies in the tens-of-MeV range, whereas the main oval can be explained without invoking such high-energy electrons.These results place new constraints on the energy and depth of electron precipitation in Jupiter’s aurora and demonstrate the unique capability of MWR multi-frequency measurements to diagnose deep ionospheric structure, complementing ultraviolet, infrared, and radio occultation observations.
presentations.session_title: Planetary magnetosphere-ionosphere coupling: aurorae and their magnetospheric/ionosphere counterparts

presentations.presentation_title: Fine-scale Auroral Injections at Jupiter and the Magnetospheric Dynamics
presentations.abstract: Jupiter’s powerful auroral emissions include a substantial component from the region at lower latitudes than the main auroral oval, named outer auroral emission. Besides the persistent auroral footprint of Jupiter’s natural moon Io, auroral injection are often observed in the outer auroral region, manifesting the magnetospheric plasma injection from middle/outer magnetosphere to the inner magnetosphere. Magnetospheric plasma injections sometimes have auroral counterparts, while sometimes have not. It is yet to be understood what controls the auroral counterparts of magnetospheric plasma injections. In this presentation, we show a long-lasting auroral injection events captured by the Hubble Space Telescope, together with simultaneous particle measurements from the Juno spacecraft. Multiple auroral substructures were identified in the injection region, which are likely associated with the observed filament plasma injections. Highest ever global numerical simulation, for the first time reproduced the massive auroral injection event. The multiple datasets and mesoscale-resolving global simulation provides key insights to understand the plasma injection processes and associated auroral emissions.

presentations.presentation_title: Longitudinally Dependent Precipitation Loss at Earth and Jupiter
presentations.abstract: The non-dipolar nature of planetary magnetic fields introduces significant longitudinal asymmetries in the loss of energetic electrons to the upper atmosphere. On Earth, intense precipitation loss is often attributed to rapid pitch-angle diffusion via resonant wave-particle interactions, while the broader landscape of electron loss dynamics is frequently governed by the “windshield wiper” effect: a combination of moderate diffusion rates and azimuthal drift, directly enhancing precipitation over the so-called South Atlantic Anomaly. This study employs quasi-linear simulations to explore the similarities and differences in longitudinally dependent precipitation signatures at Earth and Jupiter. By applying statistical whistler-mode wave environments, we characterize how low-altitude electron dynamics are moderated by wave-particle interactions and non-uniform magnetic topologies. Furthermore, we investigate the unique role of Jupiter’s rotational dynamics, specifically assessing how sub-corotational and super-corotational drift, in addition to magnetic drifts, influences the global distribution and efficiency of precipitation loss. These results aim to provide a comparative framework for understanding magnetosphere-ionosphere coupling across different planetary environments, identifying how and where electrons deposit their energy into the atmosphere.

presentations.presentation_title: Radio and Auroral Diagnostics of Planetary Magnetospheres: Solar System and Beyond
presentations.institution: Southern University of Science and Technology
presentations.abstract: Radio and auroral observations are key diagnostics of planetary magnetospheres. Giant planets such as Jupiter and Saturn emit intense radio emissions associated with magnetic reconnection, plasma waves, and electron acceleration, providing constraints on magnetic field topology, plasma distributions, and energy dissipation. Auroral emissions trace magnetosphere–ionosphere coupling, with their morphology and variability reflecting particle precipitation processes. Radio observations offer long-term monitoring of magnetospheric activity, while ultraviolet auroral imaging reveals spatial and temporal evolution. Extending these diagnostics beyond the Solar System, magnetohydrodynamic simulations of exoplanets, including TRAPPIST-1e, predict stellar wind–magnetosphere interactions capable of producing detectable radio emissions and influencing atmospheric shielding. Together, observations and modeling establish a unified framework for comparative studies of planetary magnetospheres.

presentations.presentation_title: Radio Absorption in the Martian Ionosphere During Space Weather Events
presentations.abstract: The lower ionosphere of Mars acts as an effective absorber of high-frequency (HF) radio waves during space weather events. During solar energetic particle (SEP) events, the high-energy particle precipitation into the Martian atmosphere leads to ionization at low altitudes below ~100 km, where HF radio waves can be significantly attenuated due to electron-neutral collisions. This process is analogous to polar cap absorption at Earth, but SEP precipitation and radio absorption can be global at Mars owing to the absence of a strong dipole magnetic field. Similarly, enhanced solar X-rays during solar flares can result in HF radio absorption over the entire dayside of Mars in an analogous manner to short-wave fadeout or the Dellinger effect at Earth. The enhanced HF radio absorption during space weather events may become problematic if future exploration crews are to utilize HF radio for long-range communication on Mars. Here, we outline what has been revealed by orbiter observations at Mars regarding HF radio absorption in the Martian lower ionosphere and discuss future directions.

presentations.presentation_title: Memory Effects in Jovian Radio Bursts: a Stochastic Analysis of Long-term Observations
presentations.abstract: Jovian radio bursts are transient emissions generated by energetic processes within Jupiter’s magnetosphere. These are primarily driven by interactions with its moons, the solar wind, and the planet’s rotation. Characterizing the temporal structure of these bursts is important for understanding Jovian plasma dynamics. This includes magnetosphere and ionosphere coupling as well as planetary space weather. Previous studies have focused on flux intensity, spectral morphology, and occurrence statistics. The temporal correlations and potential memory effects in Jovian radio burst activity remain poorly explored. In this study, we aim to investigate Jovian radio bursts using a non-Markovian stochastic framework that explicitly accounts for memory effects. Similar stochastic approaches have revealed correlation structures in complex natural systems, including atmospheric variability, sea-surface temperature records, seismic activity, and solar phenomena. Here, we explore the applicability of this framework to planetary radio emissions. We analyze observations from NASA’s Radio JOVE Archive together with data contributed by a global network of citizen science observers. For events with available spectrograms, time-series data are extracted using Python-based image processing techniques. To reduce instrumental and site-dependent variability, values are normalized across observing stations. Individual burst events are segmented according to burst type and inferred source region to isolate time-series fluctuations. Stochastic white noise analysis with memory is then applied using mean square displacement (MSD) to characterize temporal variability and examine the presence of correlation structures. This study presents a methodological framework for the stochastic analysis of Jovian radio burst activity. The approach provides a foundation for ongoing and future investigations of temporal correlations in Jupiter’s radio emissions and supports the continued development of community-driven observations in planetary radio astronomy.

presentations.presentation_title: Recent Results from Juno
presentations.abstract: Juno has transformed our view of Jupiter through major discoveries about its interior structure, origin, and evolution; atmospheric dynamics and composition; magnetic dynamo; and polar magnetosphere. The natural evolution of Juno’s polar orbit brings new regions within reach with every close passage to Jupiter, as the inbound equator crossing marches ever closer to the giant planet. Juno’s extended mission began in August 2021 and provided the first close flybys of Io, Europa and Ganymede since the Galileo mission. The extended mission continues providing opportunities for Juno to probe previously unexplored regions, and to follow up on Juno’s discoveries made during its prime and initial extended missions. As the mission continues, Juno dives deep into Jupiter's inner radiation belts, where the rings and inner moons reside, providing an opportunity to investigate these components and their complex interaction, yielding a unique data set to compare with other giant planet ring systems, including the ice giants. Juno’s polar perijoves provide the opportunity to continue the exploration of Jupiter’s circumpolar cyclones over a wide range of altitudes/depths via imagery, occultations and microwave sounding. Radio science occultations will characterize the upper atmosphere to levels as deep as 0.5 bar. Gravity passes over the north polar region will constrain the depth and mass of the polar cyclones and will also be compared to MWR's sounding of the same. An overview of the major results from Juno including recent results obtained will be presented.

presentations.presentation_title: Juno Microwave Radiometer Observations of Europa’s Sub-surface Ice
presentations.abstract: In late 2022, Juno’s Microwave Radiometer (MWR), collected data over a longitude range from 70 o W to 50 o E and a latitude range from ~20 o S to ~50 o N, at frequencies of 0.6, 1.2, 2.5, 5.2, 10, and 22 GHz. These observations allow us to constrain the depth and subsurface structure of Europa’s ice shell. The thickness of the thermally conductive part of the ice shell is constrained by the observed temperature gradient, and pores or cracks beneath the surface scatter microwaves, enabling us to characterize the size and distribution of the scatterers. Assuming pure water ice, our best-fit model has conductive ice shell thickness 29±10 km, negligible surface reflectivity, volume fraction of scatterers 0.045, scale height of scatterers 219 m, and scatterer size distribution power law index -3.96. Based on the size, depth, and volume fraction of the scatterers, they alone are not likely to provide a path for nutrients to travel between the ocean and the surface. Ice salinity of 15 mg/kg could reduce our estimate of the thickness by about 5 km. A thermally convective layer would slightly decrease our estimate of the conductive layer, while increasing our estimate of the total thickness. We will discuss these and other complications, as well as next steps.

presentations.presentation_title: Lava Lakes on Io: Crust Age and Implications for Thermal Output
presentations.abstract: Recent observations by NASA’s Juno mission have revealed that many of Io’s volcanic hot spots are in fact lava lakes, characterized by a colder central crust surrounded by a hotter peripheral ring. In this study, we investigate the thermal properties of about twenty such lava lakes, providing new constraints on their structure and energy budget. Our analysis shows that these features contribute a much larger fraction of Io’s total thermal emission than previously estimated. We also explore the relationship between the average temperature of the crust and the evolutionary state of each lake, offering insights into the frequency of resurfacing processes. Finally, we propose an improved assessment of Io’s global thermal output, but we emphasize that only observations that cover the full surface with sufficient spatial resolution can yield realistic values for the planet’s volcanic total heat flux.

presentations.presentation_title: Nature of Eruptions within Io's Volcanic Paterae: Lava Lake Overflows
presentations.abstract: Volcanic paterae, depressions similar to calderas, are found across Jupiter’s moon Io and serve as the main mode of heat release for the body. They have flat floors adjacent to and below surrounding level plains, and their compositions are mafic to ultramafic, meaning lavas are highly fluid. The great sizes of paterae (average diameter of 42 km) suggest large volumes of magma, should they fill, yet evidence for how patera floors might become covered in lava was not present from Galileo data. New observations from the Juno JIRAM infrared instrument revealed hot rings interior to dozens of patera margins, suggesting lava overtops a cooler crust from the margin. JunoCam visible range images show dark material where the infrared bright rings are, consistent with the emplacement of new lava. One model for the hot ring formation involves tidal pistoning of a cool, somewhat rigid crust atop a lava lake interior, causing the lava to overflow at the edges. Rather than an occasional eruption from a deep magma chamber slowly resurfacing patera floors, it appears that crusted over lava lakes are abundant within Io’s paterae, and that the lava becomes exposed at the patera margins. This requires significant volumes of lava near the surface not yet quantified and not predicted from previous observations. This would result in a crust with a significant melt volume, possibly directly related to the areal coverage of all active paterae of 1-2% of the surface.

presentations.presentation_title: Pickup Ions from the Icy Moons’ Exospheres: New Views from Juno
presentations.abstract: Juno recently performed close flybys of Europa and Ganymede, providing an exciting new window into their interactions with Jupiter’s magnetosphere. In-situ measurements of the electron distributions and ion composition provide new insights on the evolution of the surfaces and exospheres of these bodies. Notably, Juno has observed highly non-Maxwellian, anisotropic electron distributions near both moons, which we will highlight in this presentation in the context of electron-exosphere reactions. Juno has also directly observed and compositionally distinguished endogenic pickup-ions originating from the moons’ exospheres and exogenic magnetospheric ions in their immediate vicinity. By analyzing both plasma populations, we constrain the flow fields around these moons, provide constraints for the loss of exospheric material, and investigate exogenic contamination of the moons’ surfaces with Io-genic material. We will conclude with a discussion on how these plasma constraints relate to our understanding of exospheric evolution and space weathering processes at Europa and Ganymede.

presentations.presentation_title: Io Plasma Torus Observations with the Hisaki Satellite and Prospects for a Future Ultraviolet Telescope Mission LAPYUTA
presentations.abstract: The Hisaki satellite was an Earth-orbiting extreme ultraviolet (EUV) spectroscope dedicated to observing planets in the solar system. Thanks to its long-term monitoring capabilities, Hisaki carried out unprecedented continuous observations of the Io plasma torus, the Jovian aurora, and the upper atmospheres of Mars and Venus from 2013 to 2023. During the mission, Hisaki successfully observed significant enhancements in the escape of neutral gas and plasma from the active volcanic moon Io. Hisaki discovered that plasma transport and heating in the inner magnetosphere were influenced by variations in the neutral source input from Io. These variations affected the plasma environment in Europa's orbit. While Hisaki revealed the Jovian magnetosphere's dynamic characteristics, several questions remain, including the missing link between Io’s volcanic activity, neutral escape from Io, and magnetospheric plasma influence on Jovian icy moons. To address these questions, we propose the next UV space telescope: LAPYUTA (Life-Environmentology, Astronomy, and Planetary Ultraviolet Telescope Assembly). One of the goals of this mission is to study the dynamics of planets and moons in our solar system as quantifiable archetypes of extraterrestrial habitable environments in the universe. LAPYUTA will provide a UV monitoring platform with high spatial resolution and sensitivity to study the stability of Io’s atmosphere and the irradiations of the plasma to icy moons, as well as water plumes gushing from the subsurface of icy moons. It will also study the spatio-temporal aspects of Jupiter's giant UV aurora. The primary goal of the LAPYUTA mission, other than studying the Jovian system, is to study the atmospheric evolution of Venus and Mars, characterize exoplanet atmospheres, study galaxy formation, and study time-domain astronomy.

presentations.presentation_title: New Constraints on Ganymede’s Interior Properties from Improved Models of Its Permanent and Induced Magnetic Fields
presentations.abstract: Jupiter’s moon Ganymede is the only moon known to generate a global magnetic field, yet accurately modeling its internal sources is challenged by the presence of complex plasma and ionospheric currents that obscure internal signatures. This study presents refined models of Ganymede’s internal magnetic field by leveraging 3D global MHD simulations to quantify and remove these external perturbations from Galileo and Juno spacecraft data. By subtracting the simulated plasma-generated fields, we approximate a current-free environment, allowing for more precise fits of the moon’s internal moments. Specifically, using data from multiple spacecraft close flybys - including the Juno G34 pass and the previously omitted Galileo G8 pass to improve spatial coverage - we evaluate models consisting of a permanent dipole supplemented by either an induced dipole or quadrupole terms. While the permanent dipole strength remains robust at ~ 720 –727 nT (at the equatorial surface), we report a significant reduction in induction efficiency to ~ 0.72, down from the previously suggested value of 0.84. The lower induction efficiency obtained from our new analysis suggests that Ganymede’s subsurface ocean may have a lower electrical conductivity (< 1 S/m) and/or greater burial depth than earlier estimates implied. These results provide updated constraints on Ganymede’s interior and establish a new baseline for upcoming observations from the JUICE and Europa Clipper missions.
presentations.session_title: Exploring the Jovian Moons: Insights from Juno and Beyond

presentations.presentation_title: The Seven Mysteries of Callisto: a Science Case for a Next-generation Orbiter and Lander Mission
presentations.abstract: Callisto, the outermost and least evolved Galilean moon, is a primordial witness to the Jupiter system's formation that has recorded its evolution and exhibits dynamic present-day processes. In this article, we identify seven key mysteries that Callisto can illuminate: (1) the accretionary origin of the Galilean moons; (2) the early outer Solar System impact record; (3) the nature and maintenance of Callisto’s putative subsurface ocean; (4) its tidal coupling mechanisms with Jupiter; (5) the billions of years of its surface chemical evolution; (6) the dynamics of its tenuous atmosphere-ionosphere system; and (7) its unique location and potential role as a probe of Jovian magnetospheric processes. While the upcoming JUICE and Europa Clipper missions will provide critical flyby data, fully resolving these interconnected puzzles demands a dedicated mission. We detail a science traceability matrix for a mission combining a long-duration, low-altitude (200 km or less) orbiter for global geophysical and compositional mapping with a geophysics/geochemistry-focused lander. An orbiter will measure the gravity field (for moment of inertia), internal structure, tidal deformation, and global surface properties, and offer the best possible location for a magnetospheric observatory. A lander will enable such transformative investigations as very broad-band seismology, precise geodetic tracking, and direct surface chemistry measurements. This synergistic orbiter-lander architecture is the definitive path to decoding Callisto’s frozen record, answering fundamental questions about icy moon formation and degree of internal differentiation, internal oceans, and moon-magnetosphere interactions. It will ideally complement the on-going inventory of Galilean icy moons, and set a new benchmark for a deeper understanding of satellite systems across the outer Solar System.

presentations.presentation_title: Lunar Vertex: A Low-Cost Science Investigation Of The Reiner Gamma Swirl And Magnetic Anomaly
presentations.institution: Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory
presentations.abstract: Lunar Vertex, NASA’s first Payloads and Research Investigations on the Surface of the Moon (PRISM) delivery, will explore a portion of Reiner Gamma. Located in Oceanus Procellarum on the western nearside, Reiner Gamma (RG) is home to a magnetic anomaly, a region of magnetized crustal rocks. The RG magnetic anomaly is coincident with the type example of a class of irregular high-reflectance markings known as lunar swirls. Lunar Vertex will test hypotheses for the origin of swirls and magnetic anomalies, and probe the nature of solar-wind interactions with the local magnetic fields. The investigation goals will be accomplished by payload elements on a lander and on a small rover. Lander instruments: The Vertex Camera Array (VCA) is a set of cameras fixed-mounted on the lander. The Vector Magnetometer-Lander (VML) is a suite of fluxgate magnetometers. The Magnetic Anomaly Plasma Spectrometer (MAPS) measures the energy, flux, and direction of ions and electrons that reach the surface. Rover and Rover Instruments: The lander will deploy the Lunar Vertex rover, which conducts a traverse to obtain measurements both inside and outside the zone disturbed by lander exhaust. The rover carries two instruments. The Rover Multispectral Microscope (RMM) will collect images of the regolith beneath the rover at 5 wavelengths ~0.36–0.94 μm using active LED illumination. The Vector Magnetometer-Rover (VMR) is a copy of a portion of VML: an array of four mini-magnetometers. The PRISM program of rapid, low-cost, science investigations is managed under NASA NPR7120.8, which accepts higher risk and allows for substantially reduced oversight. The cost cap for Lunar Vertex is ~$30M. As part of a separate solicitation, NASA selected Intuitive Machines to provide of the Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) lander that will deliver Lunar Vertex to the Moon. Launch is planned for Q3-Q4 2026.

presentations.presentation_title: New Geologic Map of the Mare Vaporum Region
presentations.abstract: Returning to the lunar surface is a priority for several nations aiming to address key science questions and to evaluate resources that could sustain future exploration on and beyond the Moon. Identifying regions with high scientific interest and resource potential, such as pyroclastic deposits enriched in metals, oxides, water, He-3, and other volatiles, requires a comprehensive understanding of their geologic context. As geologic maps are essential for this purpose, we produced a new high-resolution geologic map of the Mare Vaporum region at a mapping scale of 1:125,000. The map reveals a diverse geology, including two distinct pyroclastic deposits likely originating from different source regions. The larger Mare Vaporum pyroclastic deposit is rich in titanium (average 8.3 ±2.0 wt%, from the TiO 2 map of Sato et al. (2017)), iron (18.8 ±1.7 wt%, from the Fe map of Lemelin et al. (2019)) and H 2 O/OH-bearing minerals (~225 ppm, Milliken & Li, 2017), which makes this region a promising candidate for in situ resource utilization. The geologic map also enables an understanding of the region’s geological history, indicating that volcanic and tectonic activity occurred between ~3.8 and ~3.2 Ga. In particular, the Rima Hyginus complex appears to have initiated around 3.8 Ga with graben formation and ended ~3.2 Ga with the deposition of pyroclastics. Graben formed until at least 3.2 Ga, suggesting that extensional stresses persisted longer than previously thought (Watters & Johnson, 2010; Watters et al., 2012).As a potential exploration site, Mare Vaporum offers favourable conditions because of its nearside location, the Eratosthenian age of its main mare unit which results in low crater density and therefore reduced landing hazards, as well as shallow slopes and minimal boulder abundance.

presentations.presentation_title: Tidal Heating of the Lunar Magma Ocean: Implications for Lunar Differentiation and Nearside–farside Dichotomy
presentations.abstract: Lunar Magma Ocean (LMO)–related samples, including ferroan anorthosites (FAN) and Mg-suite rocks, yield ages clustered near 4.35 ± 0.05 Ga, implying that the LMO remained hot for >100 Myr after Moon formation (~4.50 Ga) yet then solidified rapidly. This strongly nonlinear thermal evolution remains elusive in lunar science. We propose that this behavior arises naturally from rheology-controlled tidal heating within the LMO itself. As the LMO crystallizes, viscosity increases by orders of magnitude; both very low-viscosity melt and very high-viscosity solid dissipate tidal energy inefficiently, whereas tidal heating can increase by several orders of magnitude at intermediate viscosities when viscoelastic relaxation timescales match the tidal forcing period. Using a coupled 0-D thermal–orbital model, we obtain a long-lived stable thermal plateau in which tidal heating (>30 TW) balances heat loss, followed by an unstable thermal cliff where declining forcing and departure from the transitional rheological window shut down heating within <30 Myr. Importantly, the same mechanism can naturally generate nearside–farside asymmetry through spatially variable tidal dissipation and cooling rates, biasing crystallization timing and cumulate formation and producing hemispheric differences in residual melt, incompatible-element enrichment, and early crust–mantle structure. These results indicate that LMO evolution was governed not only by internal processes, but also by gravitational interactions between the Earth and the Moon.

presentations.presentation_title: Inverse Analysis of Mechanical Parameters in Lunar Regolith Drilling and Sampling
presentations.institution: University of Chniese Academy of Sciences
presentations.abstract: Lunar regolith drilling and sampling is a critical technology for lunar exploration and in-situ resource utilization. However, under constraints of limited energy availability and lightweight system design, the complex interactions between the coring tube and lunar regolith can readily lead to soil plugging, severely limiting coring efficiency. A thorough understanding and accurate identification of the mechanical parameters of lunar regolith during the drilling process are therefore of great scientific importance for improving sampling performance and enabling parameter-feedback optimization.Based on drilling observation data—such as weight-on-bit and vibration responses—correlative models are established to link soil properties (including friction coefficient, compaction state, and particle behavior) with sampling performance. Feedback-driven optimization of operational parameters (e.g., percussive frequency, vibration amplitude, and rotational speed) and device design is then implemented to mitigate blockage and friction while enhancing efficiency. Although conventional experimental approaches can characterize performance, they are often costly and time-consuming.To address these limitations, this study proposes a research framework that integrates experiments with machine learning. Representative datasets are collected to construct surrogate models, enabling parameter sensitivity analysis and uncertainty quantification. This work elucidates the coupling mechanisms between drilling parameters and the mechanical properties of lunar regolith, providing a new pathway for forward and inverse parameter analysis and feedback control in lunar regolith drilling and sampling, and laying a theoretical and methodological foundation for future high-efficiency coring missions.

presentations.presentation_title: Advancing Water Resource Exploration and Cislunar Science through Lunar Surface Radiation Measurement
presentations.abstract: Recent advances in high-energy astrophysics and radiation detection technology are opening new frontiers in lunar science and exploration. This presentation introduces the Moon Moisture Targeting Observatory (MoMoTarO) project, a Japanese-led initiative that integrates particle physics, radiation measurement, and planetary science to pioneer a unique interdisciplinary approach to cislunar exploration.The MoMoTarO project aims at non-contact subsurface water exploration. By utilizing a compact, high-precision neutron and gamma-ray detection system combined with detailed Monte Carlo simulations, we demonstrate the potential to quantify the abundance and depth distribution of lunar water—a critical factor for lunar geology, geophysical interpretation, and future In-Situ Resource Utilization (ISRU).Beyond resource evaluation, MoMoTarO aims to conduct high-energy space experiments that leverage the unique environment of the Earth-Moon system. Our scientific objectives include the measurement of neutron lifetime using lunar orbiters, the observation of Gamma-Ray Bursts (GRBs) utilizing the long baseline between the Earth and the Moon, and the measurement of solar neutrons originating from solar flares.The project is moving forward with a strategic roadmap: a model of the detection system is scheduled for space demonstration aboard the International Space Station (ISS) in FY2026. Furthermore, we are currently developing a detector for a lunar landing mission targeted for around 2030 under the framework of the Japanese government’s "Space Strategy Fund."

presentations.presentation_title: Exploration of lunar subsurface caverns via vertical holes: Science objectives and a mission concept building on SLIM project
presentations.abstract: We present the scientific significance and exploration potential of lunar subsurface caverns accessed through vertical holes discovered by the SELENE (Kaguya) mission in 2009. These “hole” features, tens of meters in diameter and depth, are interpreted as entrances to subsurface caverns and are those we distinguish from simple collapse features (“pits”).Shielded from micrometeoroid impacts, radiation, and extreme temperature variations, subsurface caverns can preserve pristine geological and geophysical records. The walls of vertical holes expose well-preserved natural outcrops, providing rare access to otherwise inaccessible lunar stratigraphy and making them high-priority science exploration targets.A key objective of lunar subsurface cavern exploration is to investigate evidence for an ancient lunar magnetic activity. Apollo samples suggest a strong field (10–100 μT) at 3.9–3.6 Ga, but its longevity and origin remain debated. Less-disturbed subsurface cavern environments could preserve remanent magnetization more faithfully, analogous to terrestrial lava tubes. Another objective is to constrain lava temperatures and cooling histories using mineral geothermometers and physical measurements such as the spacing of lava stalactites on cavern ceilings.Vertical-hole walls also may record lunar volatile and volcanic histories. Recent studies suggest higher interior water content than previously thought, and thin lava layers may reflect volatile-driven eruptions. Detection of iron dioxides would support water-rich magmatism, while regolith thickness and radiometric dating could constrain regolith growth and impact rates.We propose a mission concept in which an explorer descends directly into a vertical hole to dispatch robotic probes, then ascends and lands nearby to send the data attained, building on precision landing and collaborative exploration of mini probes successfully demonstrated by the 2024 SLIM mission. Finally, we outline a phased exploration strategy and propose an integrated Moon–Mars framework, “Unprecedented Zipangu Underworld of the Moon/Mars Exploration (UZUME),” combining science exploration, technology demonstration, and preparation for future base construction.

presentations.presentation_title: On the Origin of Polar Planets Around Single Stars
presentations.abstract: Binaries occur in many astrophysical systems, from young protostellar binaries in star forming regions to supermassive black hole binaries in galaxy centers. In many cases, a circumbinary disk of gas forms around the binary with an orbit that may be misaligned to the binary plane. Misaligned disks around nearly circular binaries evolve into disks that are either aligned or counteraligned with the binary orbit. However, if the binary is sufficiently eccentric, then it can be more likely that the disk ends up in a polar-aligned configuration in which the disk angular momentum vector aligns with the binary eccentricity vector. We use Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics simulations, evolved to an approximate steady state under mass injection, to determine the orbital evolution of a binary with a polar-aligned disk for a range of binary-disk parameters. We find that, in all of the cases we have simulated, the binary shrinks with time. The decay rate is larger than for binaries surrounded by aligned or retrograde disks with matched disk parameters. The rate of shrinkage is largely unaltered by the size of the sink radii employed for the binary stars, but for small enough sink radii some of the models exhibit long-lived polar circumprimary disks, which are continually fed mass from the circumbinary disk. We discuss our results in the contexts of planet formation in young polar-aligned disks.

presentations.presentation_title: Role Of Fe(ii)-Saponite On Prebiotic Chemistry In Hydrothermal Vents Of Enceladus
presentations.institution: Earth-Life Science Institute/ Institute of Science Tokyo
presentations.abstract: The icy moons are formed from small primordial bodies with a composition similar to that of asteroids [1]. Therefore, we wondered how the complex matrix of minerals, organic matter and ices might have evolved during the differentiation phase of the moons’ formation. Among the minerals, saponite has been detected in both asteroids Ryugu and carbonaceous chondrites [2], presenting catalytic properties and crystallographic structure that might facilitate the polymerisation of prebiotic molecules such as amino acids [3]. To investigate its catalytic role in prebiotic chemistry, we used mixtures of synthetic Fe(II)-saponite [4] and organic matter formed from the reaction of formaldehyde, glycolaldehyde and ammonia solution [5]. These compounds were put under hydrothermal vent conditions relevant to Enceladus and Europa seafloor circulation. These experiments aim to explore the effect of the variation of proportions of the compounds on their co-evolution in hydrothermal conditions.Afterward, the minerals are characterised using XRD-synchrotron beam and AFM-IR spectroscopy, from the interlayer nanoscale to the microscopic scale. Additionally, both soluble and insoluble organic residues are analysed using HPLC-MS and FT-ICR MS to establish their chemical evolution from elemental bulk composition to molecular scale. We will discuss the presence and nature of organic molecules trapped within the saponite interlayers and its potential role in catalysing prebiotic molecules during the formation of the Europa ocean and its impact on the habitability potential. presentations.presentation_title: Prospects of Massive Moons in Compact Systems
presentations.abstract: Analogous to the solar system formation theories, natural satellites are expected to accompany a large fraction of exoplanets, yet their existence and properties remain largely unconstrained due to observational limitations and incomplete theoretical characterization. Previous work has found an exomoon stability limit of ~0.40 times the Hill radius of the host planet, or around 20 planet radii. However, many systems are found to be vulnerable to losing their moons due to tidal disruption or outward migration. Here, we study the long-term dynamical survivability of large exomoons in 4-body compact planetary systems with two exomoons, where exomoon stability parameters are defined as functions of varying mass, eccentricity, and star-planet/planet-moon separations. We find that star-planet separation in conjunction with mass ratios play a key role in the existence of exomoons. Further, exomoon interactions can lead to one dominating the other via destabilization and ejection. We will also be analyzing how different dynamical environments lead to tidally locked exomoons. Our numerical results can feed into climate model simulations in future applications, allowing us to understand the habitability of exomoon systems. The study also has implications for the complex dynamic environment of four body systems.

presentations.presentation_title: Geophysical Signatures of Habitability in Ocean Worlds
presentations.institution: Jet Propulsion Laboratory, California Institute of Technology
presentations.abstract: We are developing integrated geophysical and geochemical forward models incorporating the latest available thermodynamic, electrical, and rheological data for solids and aqueous systems. We use the open source PlanetProfile framework to predict the gravity, magnetic, and seismic signatures of interior features in ocean worlds. I will describe the latest innovations and how we are addressing the use of geophysical sounding as a key tool for confirming the compositional inferrences from upcoming spacecraft missions to explore the icy moons of the outer planets.

presentations.presentation_title: Toward a Comprehensive Understanding of Exoplanet Atmospheric Processes
presentations.abstract: The number of discovered exoplanets has now exceeded 6,000, demonstrating that exoplanets are ubiquitous in the universe. With the launch of the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) at the end of 2021, along with recent advances in high-resolution infrared spectrographs on large ground-based telescopes, it has become possible to obtain comprehensive atmospheric spectra spanning from visible to infrared wavelengths. By exploiting the wide range of parameter space covered by exoplanet atmospheres, we can work toward a unified understanding of the physical and chemical processes governing their atmospheres. In this talk, I will discuss the current challenges in exoplanet atmospheric characterization, including the effects of aerosols, disequilibrium chemistry, uncertainties in the validity of molecular line lists at high temperatures, and present potential approaches to overcoming these challenges.

presentations.presentation_title: Stellar Flares and Chromospheric Activity of Exoplanet Host Stars from LAMOST and Kepler/TESS
presentations.abstract: Stellar flare and coronal mass ejection activity play an important role in the habitability of planets. Based on the flare activity observed in binary star systems, it has been suggested that star-planet interactions could potentially enhance the flare activity of host stars. However, observations over the past decade have not fully supported this theoretical prediction.In this study, we analyzed 3,179 late-type stars, using Kepler and TESS light curves to identify flare activity. We then compared their chromospheric activity levels using H-alpha equivalent widths from LAMOST low-resolution spectra across three groups: flare stars, inactive stars, and exoplanet host stars. Our results show that the H-alpha distribution of exoplanet host stars is similar to that of inactive stars, rather than the group of flare stars. This suggests that stellar activity in these exoplanet systems does not behave like that in binary stars, and the presence of a planet may not necessarily make the host star more active.

presentations.presentation_title: Elastic Thickness and Surface Heat Flux Estimates for Uranus’s Major Satellites from Limb Profile Variance Spectra
presentations.institution: Southern University of Science and Technology
presentations.abstract: The Uranian satellites may harbor subsurface oceans, indicating potential for habitability. However, our understanding of the Uranian moons remains limited. In this work, we estimate surface heat fluxes using limb profile data (Thomas, 1996) for the five Uranian satellites: Oberon, Titania, Umbriel, Ariel, and Miranda, presenting the first global average heat flux estimates for all five and providing insights into their thermal and orbital evolution.The approach is to infer the flexural parameter (α) from the variance spectrum of each limb profile and use it to calculate the effective elastic thickness (T e ) and surface heat flux (F). We identify a spectral slope changepoint, whose corresponding wavelength is taken to indicate α, using the Bayesian Information Criterion method (Main et al., 1999). We then estimate T e using the plate-bending formulation and derive F by employing Fourier’s law, assuming the thermal conductivity (k) of water ice varies with temperature T, following k(T) = 651/T.Our results show Oberon has the largest α (127 km) and the lowest F (9 mW m -2 ), consistent with radiogenic heating (~8 mW m -2 ). Titania and Umbriel have low α (~25 km) and high F (66 and 110 mW m -2 , respectively), whereas Ariel and Miranda show intermediate α (45 and 57 km) and F (38 and 56 mW m -2 , respectively). Except for Oberon, F for the other four moons is much higher than radiogenic heating, suggesting an ancient heat flux supplied by mean-motion resonances (MMRs). We find that the Ariel–Titania 4:1 and Ariel–Umbriel 2:1 MMRs may provide enough heating to match the inferred heat fluxes of Ariel, Umbriel, and Titania (assuming end-member dissipation partitioning), but no matching resonance is found for Miranda. These conclusions rely on several assumptions (e.g., constant Q), so further evaluation is needed.

presentations.presentation_title: Photometric Color Evolution of Interstellar Object 3I/Atlas from the Unistellar Citizen Astronomer Network
presentations.abstract: We present time-resolved color photometry of the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS (C/2025 N1) using observations collected by citizen astronomers with Unistellar eVscopes. These compact, CMOS-based telescopes are globally distributed and enable high-cadence monitoring (Marchis et al. 2020). Since the first Unistellar detection on July 4, 2025, at G = 17.8 ± 0.3, the Network has contributed an average of ~4 observations per night, forming one of the most sustained ground-based monitoring campaigns of this object. Although eVscopes do not employ standard photometric filters, recent calibration work (Perrocheau et al. 2025) enables the transformation of Bayer color channels into the Johnson–Cousins system. We apply this method to derive B, V, and R fluxes and construct time-resolved color indices (e.g., B–V, V–R). Prior to perihelion and before the onset of detectable outgassing, 3I/ATLAS appears dust-dominated and red, with colors similar to outer solar system bodies such as Centaurs. As the comet approached perihelion at ~1.36 AU in late October 2025, increasing activity consistent with water-ice sublimation was observed, which we expect to drive measurable color changes. Our high-cadence monitoring spans nearly the entire apparition, excluding the interval when the comet was unobservable near perihelion due to solar conjunction, capturing the full color evolution of this interstellar visitor. This work also highlights the capability of distributed citizen-science networks to deliver sustained, color monitoring of small bodies. References: Marchis et al. (2020), Acta Astron, 166, 23–35, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.actaastro.2019.09.028 Perrocheau et al. (2025), JATIS, 11(2), 028002, https://doi.org/10.1117/1.JATIS.11.2.028002

presentations.presentation_title: Detection of VLF Radio Emission from Bright Meteors and reentering Spacecraft
presentations.institution: National Institute of Information and Communications Technology
presentations.abstract: The presence of radio emission in the very low frequency region, including the VLF band (3-30 kHz), during the displays of meteors or reentering spacecraft has not been confirmed yet, owing to the difficulty in sorting out the background “sferics” of lightning origin. A trial of VLF observation upon the reentry of the sample-return capsule (SRC) of Hayabusa-2 was performed in December 2020 in Australia by using single loop antenna. After careful identification of sferics based on their spectral and waveform characteristics, we found several weak and non-impulsive radio signals having a close-distance origin during the fireball phase of the reentry. To confirm this finding, single-station direction-finding (DF) observation in the VLF band by using a set of NS/EW loop antennas and a vertical rod antenna was performed during the reentry of OSIRIS-Rex's SRC, taken place in the Nevada-Utah area on 24 September 2023 (UTC). Measured incident angles (azimuths) of more than twenty non-sferic radio signals largely followed the estimated azimuths based on a practical trajectory model of the SRC. A trial of the two-station DF observation, which enables us to pinpoint the geographical location of the radio source, was performed in Japan for the extremely bright fireball appearing over the Kuril Islands on 4 December 2024. The geographical locations of the fireball display estimated respectively from radio and video observations showed a remarkable coincidence. These examples of VLF radio observations give clear evidence for the presence of VLF radio emission from reentering spacecraft or bright meteors. The origin of the VLF radio emission is suggested to be the electric discharge in the highly turbulent environment of plasma formed by meteors or reentering spacecraft moving in the upper atmosphere at speeds of >10 km/sec.

presentations.presentation_title: Thermal Inertia Estimation of Small Asteroids by Light Curve Phase Lags
presentations.abstract: Thermal inertia plays a crucial role in determining the strength of the Yarkovsky effect, which drives the orbital evolution of asteroids. Recent studies have revealed that the thermal inertia of small asteroids (less than 100 meters in diameter) is one to two orders of magnitude lower than what would be expected from the trend observed in larger asteroids. However, with thermal inertia estimates for only five such asteroids to date, a larger sample is necessary for robust statistical analysis. The standard method for deriving thermal inertia requires multiple observations at different solar phase angles. This requirement presents a major bottleneck to increasing the sample size for small asteroids, as completing such observations is challenging within their short observing windows during close approaches with the Earth (typically a few days). To overcome this bottleneck, we propose a new method to estimate thermal inertia by using the phase lags between light curves observed at different wavelengths. Radiation from an asteroid consists of two components: reflected sunlight (visible light) and thermal radiation (mid-infrared light). An asteroid’s thermal light curve reflects its surface temperature distribution. For this work, we first calculated visible and mid-infrared light curves through numerical simulations. By plotting the resulting phase lags on a novel “lag-lag diagram”, which has axes representing the 20 µm vs. 7 µm and 7 µm vs. visible phase lags, we found a strong correlation between an asteroid’s position on the diagram and its thermal inertia. Based on this strong correlation, we have developed a new method to estimate thermal inertia from the two light curve phase lags, the solar phase angle, and the rotation state. This new method will enable the estimation of thermal inertia within the short observing windows, significantly increasing the sample size of thermal inertia estimates for small asteroids.

presentations.presentation_title: The Juno Spacecraft as a Novel Dust Detector: Interplanetary Dust and Passage Through a Comet Tail
presentations.abstract: A star camera aboard the Juno spacecraft traveling from Earth to Jupiter serendipitously recorded the impact of interplanetary dust particles (IDPs) by imaging bits of the spacecraft ejected from the IDP impact sites. In essence, the Juno spacecraft, with its expansive ~60 m 2 of solar arrays, served as a dust detector with orders of magnitude more aperture than dedicated dust detectors specifically designed and flown to detect dust impacts. Consequently, Juno recorded many impacts with the larger (few to tens of micro-meters) and less numerous IDPs that populate the inner solar system, establishing for the first time their distribution and source (Jorgensen et al., 2020). Six months prior to its arrival at Jupiter, the Juno spacecraft recorded a singular burst of interplanetary dust particle impacts attributed to passage through the extended tail of a comet. That comet has now been identified as the recently discovered Jupiter family comet P/2019 S3 Pan-STARRS (SPKID 1003641), affording a unique opportunity to characterize the dynamical motion of the comet’s dust tail. Dust impacting the spacecraft orbits under the influence of radiation pressure forces and gravity (ratio b = ~0.05), escaping the comet nucleus ~2 years prior to impact on the spacecraft and ~1 year post comet perihelion. Impacting dust, with an implied radius of ~10 mm, escaped the comet nucleus with a radial velocity of ~120 ms -1 , appropriate to a comet with a radius of a few km.

presentations.presentation_title: Meteor Clusters and Thier Inplications
presentations.abstract: Thanks to the increasing sensitivity of video imaging for meteor observations, including the Subaru-Asahi Cameras, meteor cluster events in which numerous meteors appear in an extremely short period of time, are now being captured with considerable frequency, and the number of samples is increasing. Comparing previous observations, we noticed that the luminosity distribution, or mass distribution, can typically be divided into two types. One type has a nearly flat mass distribution, namely most meteors are equvalent brightness, and the other is a very bright meteor followed by a series of fainter meteors. We dubbed the former a "fragmentation of monodisperse particles" type and the latter an "exfoliation" type. We will discuss the causes of these types of differences and their potential for providing important insights into the accumulation process of particles and pebbles in protoplanetary disks.

presentations.presentation_title: Utilizing Machine Learning for Gravity Inversion and Gravity Coefficient Prediction
presentations.institution: Institute of Space Technology and Space Applications, Bundeswehr University, Munich, Germany , Germany
presentations.abstract: Phobos’s unresolved origin is one of the central motivations for the upcoming Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission. MMX aims to provide the most precise constraints on Phobos’s gravity field and rotational state. These constraints are often used to directly constrain the interior structure of the associated body and therefore its evolutionary history. However, current performance estimates indicate that the mission’s gravity solution may be resolved up to degree and order 5.Therefore, this study develops a supervised machine-learning framework with two complementary learning objectives. First, we formulate gravity inversion as a classification problem by discretizing Phobos’s interior into distinct classes based on structural features, e.g., anomaly content and the form and material of subsurface structures associated with the Stickney impact. We then use gravitational coefficients, moments of inertia, and libration amplitude to predict these structures. Second, we address the expected measurement limitation by posing a regression task that predicts gravitational coefficients up to degrees and order 6–10 from moments of inertia, libration amplitude, and coefficients up to degree and order 5 (the highest order anticipated to be measurable by MMX) to further constrain plausible interiors consistent with low-degree data. We train on a large synthetic dataset (>550k instances) generated using a voxel mascon approach based on the Ernst shape model. Each instance represents a distinct interior composition (e.g., baseline interiors, anomaly fractions and distributions, and impact scenarios).Our results demonstrate that, across a variety of models and metrics, Extreme Gradient Boosting provides the strongest overall performance, reaching accuracies up to 99.7% for inversion and mean absolute percentage errors below 1.19% for coefficient prediction. This highlights an ML-assisted approach to interpret MMX constraints in terms of plausible interior structure and to estimate higher-degree coefficients for MMX and follow-on missions.

presentations.presentation_title: FOSSIL-SSR: Probing The Solar System’s Next Frontier With The Subaru Telescope
presentations.abstract: Sednoids—trans-Neptunian objects with semimajor axes a > 200 au and perihelia q > 60 au—represent one of the most dynamically pristine populations in the Solar System. Their long-term orbital stability allows them to act as fossils of the Solar System’s earliest dynamical environment, preserving signatures of processes such as stellar flybys, unseen distant planets, or the past presence of a rogue planet. However, progress has been limited by extreme observational scarcity: only four sednoids (Sedna, 2012 VP113, Leleakuhonua, and 2023 KQ14) are currently known. We present FOSSIL-SSR (Formation of the Outer Solar System: an Icy Legacy - Subaru Sednoid suRvey), a dedicated Subaru/Hyper Suprime-Cam program designed to expand the sednoid sample and test competing formation scenarios. Our program images eight carefully selected fields using the HSC-r2 filter, covering a total of 12 deg^2. Discovery observations are carried out in mid-February, with recovery observations in mid-April. Leveraging Subaru’s depth and a deep-learning-based shift-and-stack algorithm, we reach a limiting magnitude of m_r ≈ 26.9, well beyond the reach of past and ongoing TNO surveys. Our sednoid model predicts the detection of ~2 new sednoids, potentially increasing the known population by 50%, along with a comparable number of extreme TNOs and hundreds of objects from other dynamical classes. Here we present an update on the survey, including all identified sednoid candidates and plans for one-year follow-up observations to further refine their orbits and confirm their dynamical classifications. Even this modest increase in sednoid statistics provides meaningful leverage on key diagnostics, particularly the presence of primordial orbital clustering.

presentations.presentation_title: The Macro Instrument Aboard M-MATISSE: Scientific Objectives and Operational Concepts
presentations.abstract: The M-MATISSE mission, currently undergoing its Phase A study with the European Space Agency (ESA), is a candidate for the Medium-class (M7) program. Its primary objective is to study the complex interactions between Mars' magnetosphere, ionosphere, and thermosphere—commonly referred to as MIT coupling.The mission features identical payloads aboard twin spacecraft named Henri and Marguerite. These spacecraft will conduct regular mutual occultations while following elliptical orbits that share a common pericenter at an altitude of 250 km but have distinct apocenters at 3,000 km and 10,000 km, respectively.Using software-defined radios (SDRs) transmitting simultaneously at 500 MHz and 2300 MHz, the MaCro instrument, a crosslink radio science instrument, will probe the Martian ionosphere and neutral atmosphere. This approach will enable the retrieval of vertical profiles of electron density in the ionosphere, as well as temperature, pressure, and neutral number density profiles in the neutral atmosphere as well as the total lateral electron content (LTEC) and the vertical electron content (VTEC)—across nearly all local times and solar zenith angles (SZA). The orbit geometry uniquely allows coverage of SZAs less than 50° and greater than 140°, which was previously unachievable with conventional Earth-based occultation techniques, such as those used by Mars Express MaRS.Over the course of the primary mission phase (lasting one Martian year), approximately 3,000 mutual occultation events are expected to be recorded. The radio link operates in a one-way mode, with either Henri or Marguerite serving as the transmitter while the other receives the signal in open-loop mode. Onboard pre-processing of the data will reduce the volume of information transmitted back to Earth via telemetry.

presentations.presentation_title: Science Objectives of OPENS-0, a Small-spacecraft Demonstration Mission for Outer Planet Exploration
presentations.abstract: The OPENS (Outer Planet Exploration by Novel Small Spacecraft) program of JAXA aims to make outer planet exploration possible by leveraging Japan’s experience with small deep-space spacecraft. It envisions a frequent launch of small spacecraft using the Epsilon-S launch vehicle and rideshare opportunities. As the first mission of this program, the OPENS-0 has been proposed. In the original proposal, OPENS-0 is planned to be launched around 2028 by the Epsilon-S rocket, perform gravity assists at Venus and Earth, and reach the Saturnian system around 2039. OPENS-0 is currently a pre-project candidate, and studies are ongoing in preparation for the mission definition review.The primary objective of OPENS-0 is to demonstrate in space the technologies required for outer planet exploration. At the same time, the mission aims to obtain scientific results by utilizing onboard engineering instruments. During the cruise phase, the following observations may be conducted:- Acquisition of reference data for exoplanet observations through Earth photometry- Radio occultation observations of the Venusian atmosphere and the solar corona- Observations of zodiacal light and scattered cosmic background radiation at heliocentric distances from 0.7 to 10 AU- Direct measurements of the spatial distribution of interplanetary dust at heliocentric distances from 0.7 to 10 AU- Asteroid flyby observationsDuring the Saturnian system flyby, integrated observations of the rings will be carried out by combining multiple methods that target different physical quantities and spatial scales, with the aim of advancing our understanding of the formation and evolution of the rings. Candidate observations include measurements of fine ring structures and ring particles using a visible camera, characterization of the global ring structure and localized high-resolution observations through radio occultation, and direct measurements of the dust distribution from the ring region to interplanetary space.

presentations.presentation_title: Exospheric Sensing with the NASA Carruthers Geocorona Observatory
presentations.abstract: The Carruthers Geocorona Observatory, a NASA Heliophysics Science Mission of Opportunity, was launched in September 2025, and inserted into its halo orbit around the Earth- Sun L1 Lagrangian equilibrium point in January 2026. The GeoCoronal Imager onboard the Carruthers mission will obtain both narrow- and wide-field images of exospheric hydrogen emission at 121.6 nm (Lyman alpha) at unprecedented spatial resolution and temporal cadence throughout its two-year primary mission lifetime. State-of-the-art radiative transfer modeling and computational imaging will be used to retrieve the underlying hydrogen density distribution and thereby advance understanding of exospheric climatology, including long term atmospheric evolution driven by the escape of hydrogen atoms to interplanetary space. Meanwhile, measurements of transient exospheric variability during geomagnetic storms will provide unprecedented constraints on the ion-neutral coupling that mediates magnetospheric energy dissipation and promotes plasmaspheric recovery. In this talk, we will present a brief overview of the mission data products and discuss highlights of the data to date, as the team works with NASA for a public release of the data in late 2026.

presentations.presentation_title: Shadows: a Small Mission to Map the Composition of Lunar Permanently Shadowed Regions
presentations.abstract: This paper presents SHADOWS, a small satellite mission concept designed for the scientific investigation of the retention of volatiles, especially water, in permanently shadowed regions. This is a key issue for assessing the viability of these regions for in situ resource utilization for future human habitats. While these regions are protected from UV radiation and solar wind sputtering, they are continually bombarded by the sporadic background of interplanetary dust and meteoroid showers. The SHADOWS mission concept is discussed to provide the first-ever observations of the dust influx to the Moon’s polar regions and directly measure the ejecta production and subsequent gardening rates in the polar regions, which are critical to gauge their efficiency in retaining volatiles. The primary payload is an impact-ionization dust instrument, the engineering copy of the Lunar Dust Experiment (LDEX) of NASA’s Lunar Atmosphere and Dust Environment (LADEE) mission.

presentations.presentation_title: From Earth to Jupiter: In-flight Commissioning and Early Science from the MAJIS Instrument on Juice
presentations.abstract: MAJIS (Moons and Jupiter Imaging Spectrometer) is the visible and infrared imaging spectrometer onboard ESA’s Jupiter Icy Moons Explorer (JUICE) mission. It is primarily designed to investigate the composition of Jupiter’s atmosphere and the compositional properties of the icy satellites surface and exosphere. During the first 3 years of the 8.5-year interplanetary cruise to the Jovian system, MAJIS underwent a series of in-flight commissioning, performance validation and scientific activities including observations acquired during gravity-assist flybys of the Earth–Moon system and of the interstellar object Atlas/3I. These cruise-phase operations provided critical opportunities to assess instrument functionality, radiometric peformance, spectral verification, and calibration strategies under representative flight conditions. Observations of the Earth and Moon were specifically used to verify spectral registration, signal-to-noise performance, and straylight behavior, as well as to validate end-to-end processing chains using well-characterized targets. Beyond calibration and validation purposes, these observations also provided an unique opportunity to study these planetary bodies with MAJIS’s distinctive combination of spectral resolution, spectral range, and spatial resolution. In this context, we present scientific investigations of Earth’s atmosphere and the lunar surface derived from these operations. The observations of the interstellar object Atlas/3I during cruise further enabled testing MAJIS’s capability to acquire scientifically relevant measurements of transient and faint targets; initial results from these observations will be also presented.

presentations.presentation_title: The Importance of Quality Metadata in NASA PDS4 Product Labels
presentations.abstract: High‑quality metadata are foundational to the usability, longevity, and scientific value of Planetary Data System (PDS) archives. The PDS4 Information Model (IM) enforces well‑structured metadata that provide consistency (through predictable names, units, and formats); completeness (ensuring that required key attributes are present); and clarity (combining human‑readable descriptions with machine‑readable structure). These qualities are key to search relevance, API interoperability, automated analysis pipelines, and data reuse across missions and disciplines. Successful production of such metadata begins early in instrument and mission development phases. PDS4 product labels function as the connective tissue of scientific workflows. By embedding identifiers, context, and provenance, they enable faceted search, semantic tagging, FAIR‑aligned filtering, API‑driven access, label‑based retrieval, automated pipelines, provenance tracking, and cross‑mission synthesis. This metadata‑centric approach treats labels as a contract between data producers, repositories, and users, ensuring that products remain discoverable, interpretable, and reproducible over time. Creating robust metadata is not trivial. Challenges include varying levels of optional metadata supplied by providers, incomplete product references, occasional misapplication of values, and inconsistent use among related data sets. The PDS4 IM addresses many long‑standing issues from the older PDS3 approach (e.g., ambiguous field names, missing units, inconsistent formats). It defines the classes, attributes, relationships, and constraints that govern all PDS4 labels, ensuring semantic integrity and cross‑node interoperability. Discipline‑specific extensions evolve within a governed framework that preserves compatibility and shared vocabulary. Model‑driven validation further strengthens metadata quality by enforcing completeness and correctness before products enter the archive, reducing ambiguity and minimizing redelivery cycles. Because PDS tools (validation, search) are built upon the IM, changes to the model are automatically captured within the tools. Thus, product metadata support rich indexing, linked references, and external discoverability through registries and APIs.

presentations.presentation_title: Life With The Fast Grains: MASPEX Analysis Of Hypervelocity Ice Grains
presentations.abstract: The MAss Spectrometer for Planetary EXploration (MASPEX) instrument (Waite et al., 2024) launched with Europa Clipper in October 2024 on a journey to explore Ocean World habitability. The instrument design was optimized for flyby investigations of complex natural environments with high mass resolution, rapid measurement cadence, a cryotrap to capture trace volatile samples for longer analyses with enhanced sensitivity, and automated switching between measurement of ambient gas and any ice grains (“Ice Grain Mode, IGM”). In this presentation we will give an update on the flight instrument, including preparations for Jupiter Orbital Insertion in 2030. These preparations include testing the measurement of hypervelocity ice grain impacts. To this end, we coupled the MASPEX prototype instrument with the Aerosol Impact Spectrometer (AIS) particle accelerator (e.g. Burke et al., 2023), which accelerated ~1 µm ice grains into the MASPEX prototype at velocities up to ~4 km/s. We will report on detection of transient (£ 20 ms) signals associated with production of neutral gas by ice grain impacts, including mass resolved peaks from CO 2 and isopropyl alcohol. Our results inform utilization of IGM, and future mass spectral analyses of ice grain impacts during flybys. References: Burke, S. E., Miller, M. E., & Continetti, R. E. (2023).
