presentations.presentation_title: Origin and Dynamics of Lunar Ions in the Magnetotail Lobes: Observations and Simulations
presentations.abstract: Using Kaguya data spanning 1.5 years (January 2008–June 2009), we investigated the spatial distribution and dynamics of lunar-origin ions during intervals when the Moon was located within the terrestrial magnetotail lobes. These ions were detected in the energy range of 50-1000 eV at altitudes of approximately 30–120 km on the dayside and consist mainly of heavy species such as C + , O + , Na + , Al + , K + , and Ar + . To investigate their origin and dynamics, we conducted test-particle simulations with cold ions (a few eV or less) generated at the lunar surface and in the exosphere. The results indicate that lunar-origin ions observed at spacecraft altitudes primarily originate from the Procellarum KREEP Terrane. The simulations further show that ions originating in the exosphere are more effectively energized than surface-generated ions. However, the ion energization obtained in simulations with typical lunar surface potential and lobe convection velocity is lower than that of lunar-origin ions observed at spacecraft altitudes, suggesting that additional acceleration mechanisms are required to explain the observations.

presentations.presentation_title: The Impact of Asteroid Rotation Rate and Shape on Measured Spectral Features
presentations.institution: National Space Science Center, Chinese Academy of Sciences.
presentations.abstract: Spectroscopic observations of asteroids in the solar system using telescopes represent a prevalent methodology. For most asteroids, their rotation rates are sufficiently slow to induce only minimal angular displacements (at most 1-2 degrees) during the integration time of a single spectral exposure. In contrast, for certain fast-rotating asteroids—such as the near-Earth asteroid Kamo`oalewa, the first target of China's Tianwen-2 mission, with a rotation period of only about 28 minutes—the rotation angle during the telescope's spectral acquisition integration time can be an order of magnitude larger than that of slow-rotating asteroids, potentially exceeding 60 degrees in a single spectral exposure. We constructed a laboratory setup capable of driving scaled asteroid models to rotate while simulating telescopic spectral observations. To investigate whether and how asteroid rotation rate affects the observed spectral profiles, particularly the spectral slope, we measured the visible and near-infared spectra of these asteroid models at various rotation rates. By replacing models with different shapes, similar experiments were conducted to study the influence of asteroid shape on spectral observations. Our results provide significant implications for telescopic spectral observations of fast-rotating asteroids and the developement of corresponding correction strategies.

presentations.presentation_title: Key Calibration Outcomes and Preliminary Global Maps of the Moon from Danuri/polcam
presentations.abstract: South Korea's first lunar orbiter, Danuri, carries the wide-angle Polarimetric Camera (PolCam), an instrument with the unprecedented objective of conducting the first-ever global polarimetric survey of the entire lunar surface. Its initial two-year nominal phase, concluded in February 2025, was dedicated to systematically mapping the lunar surface from a 100 km orbit across ±70° latitude in polarized light. The calibration of PolCam's raw data into scientifically meaningful products is accomplished through a comprehensive data processing pipeline. We focus here on the three key calibration processes: the mitigation of smear artifacts, the estimation of the camera model, and geometric correction to produce orthorectified images. The successful implementation of these calibration processes has led to the creation of the first global lunar map from a South Korean mission. This achievement provides a significant technical foundation for the mission's ultimate goal to create the world's first global polarimetric map of the Moon.

presentations.presentation_title: Nanomechanical Properties of Space-weathered Amorphous Rims in Lunar Regolith
presentations.abstract: Amorphous rims produced by space weathering are ubiquitous on grains from airless bodies, yet the nanoscale mechanical properties remain poorly constrained. In this study, the amorphous rim was investigated using AFM, allowing its boundaries to be precisely studied for targeted mechanical probing. QNM shows that the rim is consistently stiffer than the base minerals, providing the first direct mechanical evidence of space weathering-induced stiffening. The magnitude of stiffening decreases with rim thickness and varies systematically with the base minerals, with Fe–Ti–rich substrates exhibiting the highest moduli. These results establish the first nanoscale mechanical framework for space-weathered rims and provide a physical basis for investigating regolith mechanical of airless planetary surfaces.

presentations.presentation_title: Electrochemical Signatures of Space Weathering in Lunar Regolith
presentations.abstract: The work function of lunar soil particles provides a sensitive indicator of space-weathering processes and surface charging behavior on the Moon. In this study, we combine vacuum-environment KPFM measurements with high-resolution TEM imaging to quantify the contrast between the work function of particle interiors and their weathered rims. Our results reveal a systematic increase in work function within nanometer-scale altered layers relative to fresh cores, reflecting the accumulation of amorphous rims, nanophase iron, and defect-rich structures produced by solar wind irradiation and micrometeoroid bombardment. This electrochemical differentiation provides new geological insights into regolith maturity, surface charging heterogeneity, and electron–phonon interactions in space-weathered materials. From an engineering perspective, the identified work-function gradients have direct implications for lunar exploration and resource utilization, influencing dust adhesion, electrostatic lofting, instrument grounding, and in-situ energy-harvesting strategies. These findings establish work-function mapping as a valuable diagnostic for future lunar science and surface-operations planning.

presentations.presentation_title: Planets Across Space and Time (past). Viii. Kinematic Characterization and Identification of Radial Velocity Variables for the Lamost-gaia-tess Stars
presentations.abstract: The Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) has discovered over 6700 nearby exoplanet candidates using the transit method through its all-sky survey. Characterizing the kinematic properties and identifying variablestars for the TESS stellar sample is crucial for revealing the correlations between the properties of planetarysystems and the properties of stars (e.g., Galactic components, age, chemistry, dynamics, and radiation). Based on data from TESS, Gaia DR3, and LAMOST DR10, we present a catalog of kinematic properties (i.e., Galactic positions, velocities, orbits, Galactic components, and kinematic age) as well as other basic stellar parameters for ∼660,000 TESS stars. Our analysis of the kinematic catalog reveals that stars belonging to different Galactic components (i.e., thin disk, thick disk, halo, and 12 streams in the disk) display distinctive kinematic and chemical properties. We also found that hot planets with periods less then 10 days in the TESS sample favor thin disk stars compared to thick disk stars, consistent with previous studies. Furthermore, using the LAMOST multiple-epoch observations, we identify 41,445 stars exhibiting significant radial velocity variations, among which 7846 are classised as binary stars. By fitting the radial velocity curves, we further derive orbital parameters (e.g., mass ratio, orbital period, and eccentricity) for 297 binaries. The catalogs constructed in this work have laid a solid foundation for future work on the formation and evolution of stellar and planetary systems in different Galacticenvironments.

presentations.presentation_title: The Impact of Cold Jupiter Growth on the Formation and Survival of Short-period Low-mass Planets
presentations.abstract: The formation of cold Jupiters (CJs) can significantly reshape the structure and evolution of protoplanetary gas disks. Recent theoretical studies suggest that the growth of massive planets may modify the gas surface density distribution in the inner disk and alter global mass transport, thereby changing the migration environment experienced by low-mass planets. Understanding how these disk-level changes influence the formation and orbital evolution of short-period low-mass planets is essential for linking giant planet formation with the diversity of observed planetary system architectures. In this study, we investigate how the growth of cold Jupiters affects the formation and inward migration of short-period low-mass planets. Our goal is to explore the physical conditions under which the presence of a growing giant planet can significantly influence the migration pathways, survival, and final orbital configurations of sub-Earth- to super-Earth-mass planets. We combine analytical estimates with numerical experiments to study disk evolution and planet–disk interactions in the presence of growing cold Jupiters. First, we examine how CJ formation modifies the gas surface density profile and migration torques in representative disk models, guided by recent theoretical frameworks. We then conduct N-body simulations with parametrized disk evolution to evaluate the migration behavior and survival of low-mass planets under different CJ growth scenarios. These experiments are used to identify key controlling parameters and to refine the design of more comprehensive simulations. Our results suggest that the growth of cold Jupiters can substantially alter the migration and retention of low-mass planets by reshaping the inner disk structure and reducing inward mass flux. In certain regimes, this results in suppressed inward migration or enhanced loss of short-period low-mass planets. These findings highlight the potential role of giant planet growth in shaping the architecture of close-in planetary systems and provide a theoretical framework for future detailed simulations and observational comparisons.

presentations.presentation_title: EKL Making Resonant Sub-Neptunes Dynamically Hotter
presentations.abstract: Near-resonant Kepler planets are dynamically hot, as evidenced by their large transit timing variation (TTV) phases. Recent observations suggest that dynamically hot resonant planets represent an intermediate stage in the close-in sub-Neptune population at young ages. We investigate the possibility of TTV phase excitation of close-in resonant pairs by a cold Jupiter interacting with a stellar companion through the eccentric Kozai-Lidov mechanism (EKL). We found that the EKL model driving the observed eccentricity of cold Jupiters can excite large TTV phases and even disrupt resonant pairs in a significant fraction of planetary systems in our simulated sample.

presentations.presentation_title: CHES: a Space-borne Astrometric Mission for the Detection of Habitable Planets of the Nearby Solar-type Star
presentations.institution: Purple Mountain Observatory, Chinese Academy of Sciences
presentations.abstract: The Closeby Habitable Exoplanet Survey (CHES) is a proposed space-based astrometric mission dedicated to discovering and characterizing habitable planets around nearby solar-type stars. By delivering microarcsecond-level relative astrometry from space, CHES aims to address key questions in exoplanet science, including the occurrence rate, physical properties, and orbital architectures of Earth-like planets in the solar neighborhood.CHES will target approximately 100 F-, G-, and K-type stars within ~10 pc of the Sun and search for terrestrial planets in their habitable zones. The mission will directly measure true planetary masses and full three-dimensional orbital configurations, capabilities that transit and radial velocity techniques alone cannot uniquely provide. Based on current occurrence rate estimates and mission simulations, CHES is expected to detect roughly 50 habitable-zone terrestrial planets, enabling a statistically meaningful census of potentially habitable planets around Sun-like stars.The mission employs a 1.2 m coaxial three-mirror anastigmat telescope operating in the optical band with a 0°.44 × 0°.44 field of view. Its focal plane consists of 81 CMOS detectors, allowing simultaneous observations of target stars and multiple reference stars. To meet its astrometric precision requirement, CHES uses heterodyne laser interferometric metrology for on-orbit calibration, achieving micropixel-level detector characterization and ensuring microarcsecond accuracy.Operating at the Sun–Earth L2 point for a nominal five-year lifetime, CHES will provide a comprehensive view of nearby planetary systems, from Earth analogs to giant planets, and supply prime targets for future direct imaging missions. Beyond exoplanet science, CHES will deliver high-precision astrometry for studies of compact objects, Galactic dynamics, and dark matter through accurate proper motion measurements, representing a significant step toward understanding nearby planetary systems and fundamental astrophysical processes.

presentations.presentation_title: Free Eccentricities of Circumbinary Planets and Implications for Their Formation and Dynamical Evolution
presentations.abstract: The orbits of circumbinary planets can be significantly non-Keplerian due to the time-varying gravitational potential of the binary. The eccentricity of a circumbinary orbit is a combination of the forced eccentricity at the mean motion and the free eccentricity at the epicyclic frequency, with the latter set by the dynamical processes during the formation and evolution of the planet. We have determined the free eccentricities of all currently known circumbinary planets using frequency analysis. We find that circumbinary planets exhibit systematically low free eccentricities compared to the eccentricities of planets around single stars. Since the stability of a circumbinary orbit depends on the parameters of the binary and the orbital distance and eccentricity of the planet, we have performed Monte Carlo experiments in which the eccentricity distribution of single-star planets is filtered by the stability criterion. The resulting distributions are consistent with the free-eccentricity distribution of observed circumbinary planets, indicating that dynamical stability selection plays an important role in shaping the orbital architecture of circumbinary planetary systems.

presentations.presentation_title: White Dwarf Pollution from Planetesimals with N-body Simulations
presentations.institution: Institute for Advanced Study, Shenzhen University
presentations.abstract: White dwarfs that show heavy element pollution in their photospheres suggest that external material was accreted relatively recently through some mechanism. Therefore, white dwarf pollution provides an important clue for understanding the past and present dynamical structure of the system and the distribution of bodies around the star. Many studies have investigated the origin of white dwarf pollution. One leading scenario is the planetesimal perturbation model. In this model, planetesimals in the system are dynamically perturbed, their orbits become unstable, they are delivered to the vicinity of the white dwarf, and they finally collide with the white dwarf or are tidally disrupted and then accreted. Many different mechanisms have been proposed for what perturbs the planetesimals. Among them, one of the most plausible candidates is a massive companion, such as a planet or a substellar object, capable of inducing long-term dynamical instability. In this study, we focus on a specific and characteristic polluted white dwarf system which is known to host a companion, and test whether dynamical perturbations of planetesimals in that system can reproduce the observed white dwarf pollution. We place planetesimals around the white dwarf and consider several system configurations that include the observed companion, as well as additional bodies. We follow the long-term evolution up to 1 Gyr using N-body simulations. Our simulations show that, depending on the system configuration, an unstable region forms where planetesimals cannot survive for a long time. We also find that long lasting accretion onto the white dwarf can occur when planetesimals near the edge of the unstable region are scattered over long timescales. On the other hand, the efficiency of accretion and the characteristic timescales depend on the properties of the additional bodies in the system. This result suggests that this polluted system may host unseen bodies.

presentations.presentation_title: ESA's Exospheric Mass Spectrometer for the LUPEX Rover (EMS-L)
presentations.abstract: This presentation will summarise the plans and status of the European Space Agency's 'Exploration Mass Spectrometer' for LUPEX (EMS-L). This novel ion trap mass spectrometer is planned for flight in collaboration with JAXA on their LUPEX rover, which is set to explore the south polar region of the Moon in search of ices and volatiles. EMS-L will be able to measure volatiles and other species within the tenuous lunar exosphere, and will help to understand the environment in which the rover is completing its analyses, and assess how the rover itself is altering the environment. This will contribute to measurements of volatiles both during transit and at sites where drilling and detailed analyses are being completed. The EMS-L instrument development is led by Kayser Italia with key subcontractors Open University, RAL STFC, COMAT, and Oxford University. The mass spectrometer at the heart of EMS-L is being developed by Open University and is based on heritage from the 'EMS' instrument that flew as the core of the PITMS payload on the Peregrine-1 mission. This was the first of NASA's 'Commercial Lunar Payload Services' (CLPS) missions, launching in January 2024. Sadly, Peregrine-1 did not reach the Moon, but the scientific instrumentation was operated as much as possible during the flight, and EMS performed very well, providing an excellent technical demonstration of the instrument and some valuable data. The data and operational lessons from this first flight are being used to inform the development of an improved instrument for implementation on LUPEX. Among the innovations implemented in EMS-L are the addition of a calibration unit, the integration of an infrared surface temperature sensor, various design features that will improve the instrument’s sensitivity, and the addition of a motorized protective dust cover. EMS-L will perform periodic measurements throughout all LUPEX mission phases.

presentations.presentation_title: Understanding Thermophysical Environment of Lunar Poles: Implications to Volatile Stability.
presentations.abstract: The thermophysical environment of the Moon has been extensively studied over the past decades, particularly in the context of scientific advancements and future human exploration. Since the surface and subsurface temperatures on the Moon vary with latitude, local time, and topography, each site offers a unique insight into the lunar thermal regime. The polar regions, in particular, vary both diurnally and seasonally, exhibiting distinct thermal behaviour compared to equatorial and mid-latitude areas. These temperature fluctuations significantly impact the stability and transport of volatiles, such as water ice. Therefore, polar regions require more detailed investigation and modelling with specific parameters, particularly at regional or local scales. This study focuses on the numerical modelling of key sites at the lunar poles to better understand their thermophysical environment and consequently, the stability of volatiles in these regions.The modelling has been carried out using a 3D finite element thermophysical model. The actual topography with the highest possible resolution is used for each site. Since the solar illumination is almost at grazing angle over lunar poles, the solar flux is calculated using complex and realistic illumination, varying over time. The thermophysical parameters such as thermal conductivity, bulk density etc. are given as depth and temperature dependent functions and the surface, subsurface temperatures are calculated. The illumination conditions and temperatures are compared with remote sensing datasets and previous models and are validated. Major results of this study will be presented and discussed.

presentations.presentation_title: Preparation for Artemis Sample Return: Developing Techniques to Analyze Volatiles in Frozen Lunar Samples
presentations.abstract: Over the last two decades, remote sensing observations revealed the widespread presence of water on the surface of the Moon, which was confirmed by the analysis of returned Apollo samples. Several mechanisms have been proposed for the origin of this water, including via solar wind implantation through space weathering processes. However, our understanding of the life cycle of water and other volatiles on the Moon is still at an early stage. With the planned return of volatile-rich, frozen samples from the lunar South Pole by the NASA Artemis Missions, developing techniques to characterize their volatile content will be critical for understanding the life cycle of these species on the lunar surface. To develop this analytical pipeline, we prepared a mature space weathered ilmenite grain from Apollo 17 soil 79221 for analysis using a cryogenic focused ion beam scanning electron microscope (FIB-SEM). We collected high resolution images and electron energy-loss spectroscopy (EELS) measurements from the ilmenite FIB section using a cryogenic transmission electron microscope (TEM). We identified nanophase iron particles and microstructural defects like vesicles within the space weathered rim of the grain. We collected EELS spectra from within the vesicles to identify the presence of trapped water and hydrogen. We identified an H K-edge at ~13 eV in EELS spectra collected from within the vesicles for the first time. Looking forward, we would like to further develop this end-to-end cryogenic pipeline by transferring the sample from the FIB to the TEM in a cold glovebox. Ultimately, we will use this analytical pathway on experimentally irradiated analog samples under cryogenic temperatures and gradually warm them to ambient temperatures for analysis to understand volatile migration or loss under varying thermal conditions that might be expected on the lunar surface.

presentations.presentation_title: Exploration of Lunar Water by Lunar Thermogravimetric Analyzer (LTGA) Onboard LUPEX Rover
presentations.abstract: Lunar Polar Exploration (LUPEX) mission is a joint mission with Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) to investigate lunar water resources in the lunar polar region through in-situ observation by a rover. The rover will install seven mission instruments. The largest instrument, Resource Investigation Water Analyzer (REIWA), is a packaged instrument to analyze water and other volatiles within a lunar regolith sample acquired by a rover drilling system and consists of following subsystems: Lunar Thermogravimetric Analyzer (LTGA), Triple Reflection Reflectron (TRITON), Aquatic Detector using Optical Resonance (ADORE), ISRO Sample Analysis Package (ISAP), Common Electronics (COM-E), Common Plumping (COM-P), and Sample Container Handling System (HNDG). LTGA is the first thermogravimetric analyzer for use on a gravitational body except Earth. It can actively heat the lunar regolith sample from 100 K to 500 K in 30 minutes and weigh the sample simultaneously with a resolution of 9.8 x10 -6 N, which can detect 0.1 wt% change due to volatilization from the sample of 6 g under lunar surface gravity. An engineering model (EM) of LTGA has been manufactured and most of the functional tests have been completed. We've been conducting some further tests to maximize the LTGA outcome, such as experiments to measure the temperature and pressure dependence of the thermal properties of regolith simulant. In this presentation, we will introduce expected outcomes from LTGA observation, the development status of LTGA and the results of each test.

presentations.presentation_title: Perspectives of Water-ice/volatiles from Chandrayaan-3 and Prospects from Lupex/chandrayaan-5
presentations.abstract: The presence and distribution of lunar water-ice and other volatiles is the cornerstone of future lunar exploration, outpost activity and human habitation. While orbital remote sensing from Chandrayaan-1 and LRO established a global "inventory," of water-ice and volatiles, in-situ evidences about the distribution and true nature of these deposits (surface frost, interstitial grains, or solid slabs) is lacking. Recently ISROs Chandrayaan-3 mission has accomplished a successful soft landing at southern polar region of the Moon providing the first-ever ground truth about the surface composition, it properties and possibility of water-ice/volatiles. Although Chandrayaan-3 landed in a sunlit region, its payload suite offered pivotal constraints on volatile stability. Data from the Chandrayaan-3’s ChaSTE instrument suggests water-ice may be more prevalent than previously thought, extending into high-latitude regions beyond the deep polar craters. This has shifted the perspective on lunar water-ice from a "polar-only" phenomenon to a potentially widespread, accessible resource.The APXS and LIBS instruments on the Pragyan rover of Chandrayaan-3 mission unequivocally confirmed the presence of Sulfur (S) in the polar regolith. As a volatile element with a low sublimation point, the presence of sulphur suggests that the local geochemistry is capable of retaining volatile species over geological timescales. FOllowing Chandrayaan-3, LuPEX/Chandrayaan-5 rover will enable in-situ detection and quantification of water-ice mixed with lunar surface and subsurface soil (regolith) along the traverse of the rover. While Chandrayaan-3 mission has shifted the perspective on lunar water-ice from a "polar-only" phenomenon to a potentially widespread, accessible resource, LUPEX/Chandrayaan-5 mission is expected to provide a definitive evidence for its presence and distribution near the lunar south pole. Results about water-ice/volatiles from Chandrayaan-3 ChaSTE measurements and future prospects through PRATHIMA instruments onboard LuPEX/Chandrayaan-5 mission will be discussed.

presentations.presentation_title: Development Status of REIWA-TRITON Onboard the LUPEX Moon Rover
presentations.institution: Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency / Institute of Space and Astronautical Science
presentations.abstract: For the purpose of investigating the presence and amount of the water (ice) molecules in the regolith 1 to 1.5 m below the lunar surface, a compact neutral particle mass spectrometer TRITON (Triple-reflection Reflectron) is under development. TRITON is a sub-system of REIWA (Resource Investigation Water Analyzer) onboard the LUPEX (Lunar Polar Exploration) Moon rover. REIWA also includes two other sub-systems, ADORE (Aquatic Detector using Optical Resonance) and LTGA (Lunar Thermogravimetric Analyzer) in addition to TRITON. TRITON will perform mass analysis of the neutral gas generated by LTGA. In order to increase the mass resolution as much as possible within the allocated volume, we have decided to modify the standard reflectron by adding a second reflector that enables triple reflections and doubles the flight length (triple reflection mode). The triple-reflection TOF mass spectrometer can be operated also as a standard reflectron by changing the voltage applied to the analyzer (single reflection mode). Triple-reflection mode is suitable for high mass resolution measurement and standard single reflection mode is suitable for high sensitivity measurement. The Engineering Model (EM) analyzer of TRITON was designed and manufactured based on the test results from the Test Model (TM) analyzer, taking into account the structure adapted to the flight environment. Performance tests of TRITON EM analyzer confirmed that TRITON can measure the atoms, molecules and their isotopes up to mass number 200 with mass resolution as high as 150. Following the assembly with the electronics part, function check, EMC test, environment test including vibration test and thermal vacuum test were successfully conducted. The results of the EM tests were reflected on the design of the Flight Model. Since TRITON has passed CDR, flight model manufacturing is currently underway.

presentations.presentation_title: New Lunar Cold Spots: The Thermophysical Properties of the Youngest Craters on the Moon
presentations.institution: Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory
presentations.abstract: We report the formation of a lunar cold spot surrounding a newly discovered 225 m-diameter impact crater that formed in Spring 2024 and was identified in repeated imagery by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) Camera [1]. This is by far the largest newly identified crater to date (previously ~70 m) [2,3] and represents a century-scale event based on crater production models [4]. Nighttime temperature observations by the Diviner Infrared Radiometer on LRO reveal a ~7 km-wide cold spot with a peak temperature anomaly ~8–9 K cooler than its surroundings. We investigate the thermophysical properties and potential cold spots of this crater and 20 other new craters formed during the LRO mission [2,3,5]. We find that all new craters >30 m exhibit detectable cold spots, indicating that cold spot formation is ubiquitous for fresh lunar craters. The cold-spot temperature anomaly increases with crater diameter, suggesting that larger cold spots decompact the regolith more significantly or to greater depth. This trend plateaus for craters larger than ~100 m, possibly consistent with regolith modification depths approaching a few multiples of the diurnal thermal skin depth, beyond which additional modification has little effect on nighttime temperature. Additionally, we find that new cold spots have a greater temperature anomaly than the global population of pre-existing cold spots. This indicates that the present-day magnitudes of the cold spot temperature anomalies are primarily dominated by the cold spot size and age, while we see little evidence to suggest variations in target properties or impact conditions significantly influence the state of the anomalies. presentations.presentation_title: Scoping the Architectural Future of Extra-terrestrial Habitat Design and Construction
presentations.abstract: Need for long-duration habitation in space has become a strategic imperative for space exploration and scientific research. Establishing semi-/ or permanent human presence in space or on other celestial bodies will facilitate continuous scientific research and development, in-situ resource utilization.Extra-terrestrial environment is extremely hostile to habitation. The Moon presents extreme thermal cycles, vacuum conditions, high radiation exposure, micrometeoroid impacts, electrostatic charging, reduced gravity, and abrasive regolith, which have a critical impact on material properties, construction techniques, life support systems, and human physiological and psychological factors.Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) has been making steady progress to overcome these challenges. Chandrayaan series of missions, culminating in successful Chandrayaan-3 south polar landing, have established access to surface and provided critical terrain, thermal, plasma, and regolith information that form the basis for future habitation. Simultaneously, the ISRO plan for Gaganyaan human spaceflight program, conceptualized Bharatiya Antariksha Station, and stated goal of an Indian crewed lunar mission by 2040, heralds a shift towards permanent off-world infrastructure from current focus on short-duration missions. This requires in-situ fabrication, robotics, autonomy, environmental control, and human-centric habitat design, which extends beyond the traditional purview of aerospace engineering.Realizing this interdisciplinary requirement, the Department of Architecture and Planning (DAP), IIT Roorkee, started the process of collaboration with ISRO after the visit of ISRO Chairman. This process has now matured into expert interactions through Two-Day Brainstorming Workshop on Habitat Design and Construction on the Moon’s Surface. This effort aims to bring together architects, engineers, scientists, and biomedical professionals to define habitat design as a convergence of technology, environment, and human well-being. Based on this, IIT Roorkee and ISRO propose the Space Architecture (SpAr) Conclave 2026 and the multidisciplinary hackathon as future platforms for research to be converted into design innovation and capacity building for India’s long-term lunar habitation strategy.

presentations.presentation_title: The Photochemical (im)plausibility of Warm Exo-titans
presentations.abstract: The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has begun to spectrally characterize small exoplanets orbiting M-dwarf stars, but interpretation of these spectra is ambiguous, as apparent spectral features may have stellar, instrumental, or atmospheric origins. Consequently, interpretation of JWST small exoplanet spectra follows a Bayesian approach, with less theoretically plausible interpretations facing a higher burden of proof. Arguments from planet formation and hints from observations have been used to suggest the existence of warm exo-Titans, exoplanets with Titan-like CH 4 -rich atmospheres orbiting close to their host stars. Here, we use photochemical modeling to evaluate the plausibility of such planets. Using the candidate habitable-zone exo-Titan TRAPPIST-1e as a case study, we show that the higher instellation experienced by warm exo-Titans reduces their CH 4 lifetime τ CH4 relative to true Titan by orders of magnitude, reducing the probability of observing them. We constrain τ CH4 on a warm exo-Titan to be ≤0.1× (and most likely ≤0.02×) true Titan, implying the absolute probability of detecting a warm exo-Titan is <0.1 and likely <0.01. The low prior probability means that the standard of proof required to claim a warm exo-Titan detection is high, and we offer specific suggestions towards such a standard of proof. Observation of oxidized carbon species would corroborate a putative warm exo-Titan detection. Confirmed detection of warm exo-Titans would signal the need to fundamentally rethink our understanding of the structure, dynamics, and photochemistry of Titan-like worlds. Our work explains recent JWST observations, is the first-ever quantitative constraint on the likelihood of warm exo-Titans, and has implications for the reliability of CH 4 as a biosignature gas on exoplanets.

presentations.presentation_title: What Jwst Really Sees: Time-dependent Atmospheric Signatures
presentations.abstract: The interpretation of exoplanet spectra obtained with JWST typically assumes that observed atmospheres are in steady state. In this work, we challenge that assumption by demonstrating that stellar flares can induce rapid and long-lasting changes in atmospheric composition that directly impact observables. We model the effects of recurrent stellar flaring on metal-rich exoplanet atmospheres using time-dependent photochemistry and radiative transfer. We find that flare activity drives strong variability in key molecules such as SO₂, CO₂, CH₄, and H₂O, producing spectral changes at the tens to hundreds of parts-per-million level, well within JWST sensitivity. Extreme flares can temporarily suppress molecular features, while cumulative flaring leads to persistent compositional shifts on decadal timescales. These results imply that JWST spectra do not necessarily probe a planet’s equilibrium state, but rather a snapshot conditioned on recent stellar activity. Atmospheric retrievals must therefore account for temporal variability to avoid biased inferences of composition and climate, especially for planets orbiting active stars.

presentations.presentation_title: Multi-species Mass Fractionation on the Planets Along the Radius Valley Due to Photoevaporation
presentations.abstract: We study the mass fractionation of hydrogen, deuterium, helium, and metal in the photo-evaporating atmosphere of a sub-Neptune. Instead of using the conventional crossover mass method, we adopt an analytical approach that accounts for aerodynamic drag among multiple species simultaneously. The coupled thermal and mass-loss evolutions are then conducted for a grid of interior simulations using MESA. We will present the resulting compositions of the sub-Neptune population along the radius valley in this multi-species model.

presentations.presentation_title: Worlds Under Fading Stars: 3d Chemistry-climate Modeling of White Dwarf Exoplanets
presentations.abstract: The search for habitable environments is constantly improving with an ever-increasing ability to detect and classify exoplanets. White Dwarfs (WDs) present an incredible opportunity in studying exoplanet environments as they provide stable environments for billions of years as they cool, and their size allows for strong spectral signatures opening new possibilities in biosignature detection sensitivity. However, little is known about the climate stability and volatile composition of exoplanets orbiting WDs. Much of this uncertainty comes from the stellar cooling, time-evolving photon flux, and ultrafast synchronous rotation that distinguish WD exoplanets from more conventional host stars. Previous studies evaluating the habitability of WD exoplanets have shown that they can support the formation and existence of life over the multi-billion year timescales expected to be necessary for complex life to evolve. This is highly dependent on the energy provided to the planet by the WD, and therefore the atmospheric conditions present. Our work utilizes a 3D chemistry-coupled global climate model (WACCM) to evaluate the climate stability, retention, and circulation patterns of WD exoplanets. These novel results build on the conventional habitable zone by showing how the circulation regimes of an ultrafast synchronously rotating planet affect climate stability and the potential for escape or retention of biologically relevant gases. The inclusion of chemistry-climate interactions open new possibilities in analysis of habitable conditions, atmospheric retention, and observationally testable spectral signatures. When implemented into the generation of synthetic atmospheric spectra, they reveal unique features that future missions of JWST, ELTs, or HWO can use as a baseline for atmospheric characterization. In combination with an improved planetary evolution history and volatile inventory models, this work will provide the most complete understanding of whether WD planetary systems can host life while also informing future missions of the ideal targets to prioritize in such a search.

presentations.presentation_title: Morphological Regimes of Aggregate Hazes in Exoplanet Atmospheres
presentations.abstract: Photochemically produced floating particles—called hazes—are ubiquitous in planetary atmospheres and play a crucial role in controlling planetary climate and atmospheric observability. In particular, particle shape, often characterized by fractal dimension D f , is a critical parameter for assessing the impacts of hazes because it dictates the aerodynamic and optical properties of photochemical hazes. However, current haze studies have strongly relied on the assumption of Titan-like aggregate hazes (D f =2) or empirical relation for D f derived from soot combustion experiments, far from the environments of many exoplanetary atmospheres. In this study, we leverage the porosity evolution recipe established by the planet formation community to investigate how the morphology of photochemical hazes varies with planetary properties. Our simulations reproduce the Titan-haze morphology (D f =2) for Titan-like parameters, whereas the aggregate hazes tend to have more compact morphologies at high haze production rate, small monomer size, and low planetary gravity. We find a novel regime in which photochemical hazes rapidly grow into large, compressed aggregate particles. In the talk, we will discuss the expected morphology evolution of aggregate hazes over planetary evolution and its observational implications.

presentations.presentation_title: Coias: Search Application for Small Solar System Bodies
presentations.institution: National Institute of Technology, Matsue College
presentations.abstract: We developed a web-based application, COIAS (Come On! Impacting ASteroids), designed for the detection of Small Solar System Bodies (SSSBs) from HSC-SSP (Hyper Suprime-Cam, Subaru Strategic Program) images. The primary goal of COIAS is to elucidate the orbital and taxonomic distributions of SSSBs, many of which have remained undetected due to their small size and low albedo. In addition to advancing fundamental planetary science, COIAS contributes to planetary defense efforts by enabling the detection of near-Earth objects (NEOs). Furthermore, COIAS is expected to facilitate the discovery of active asteroids, comets, and a significant number of trans-Neptunian objects (TNOs). A key feature of COIAS is its emphasis on citizen science, which is achieved through a highly user-friendly interface that encourages public participation. As of December 2025, COIAS has detected and reported over 260,000 new objects to the Minor Planet Center (MPC), with contributions from approximately 1,000 citizen scientists. Among these detections, 8,008 objects were assigned a provisional designation. Of particular significance, COIAS holds the world record for the highest number of TNO discoveries in 2024.

presentations.presentation_title: Deimos Photometric Properties from Mars Express HRSC and SRC Observations
presentations.abstract: For more than 22 years, the Mars Express (MEx) mission has been orbiting the Martian system, acquiring data on Mars' surface and atmosphere, as well as on its two moons, Phobos and Deimos, trying to decipher the unknown origin of the Martian moons. In this study, we analyzed images of Deimos taken with the High Resolution Stereo Camera (HRSC) and its Super Resolution Channel (SRC) onboard MEx. We performed both disk-resolved and disk-resolved photometry, and applied semi-empirical radiative transfer models. The results of this analysis indicate that Deimos has a strong opposition surge, which is mainly due to shadow hiding, and likely indicate the presence of a thick dust layer and/or complex-shaped grains at the surface. We found that the coherent backscattering process is negligible on Deimos. We also observed that the craters appear to exhibit no discernible increase in reflectance compared to the average surface. This contrasts with Phobos, where the crater rims are significantly brighter (up to 50%) than the average surface, at least in the area dominated by, or close to the blue unit. This suggests that the craters on Deimos are likely relatively old. Based on the HRSC images, we have tentatively identified a blue unit on Deimos on the equatorial ridge (streamers). This blue unit on Deimos, similar to the one on Phobos, suggests a common origin for the two Martian moons. The variations between the different units may be associated with changes in surface texture, such as grain size and porosity, or space-weathering processes. This work is the first extended study of the photometric properties of Deimos, in particular covering the opposition effect. The results are of significant interest for JAXA’s Martian Moon eXploration (MMX) mission, which will launch in october 2026 and return samples from Phobos.

presentations.presentation_title: Integrating Optical Observations and Seismoacoustic Data for Monitoring Meteor Over Japan, 2025
presentations.abstract: Meteoroids of different sizes and velocities penetrate the atmosphere with a significant hazard to individuals and infrastructure. A meteoroid that entered the atmosphere on 19th August 2025 at 14:08:48 UTC is considered the largest fireball in the last decade over Japan. The meteor trajectory was derived from optical observations. Additionally, the meteor produced a shock wave that was recorded by seismic and infrasound sensors. Infrasound observations obtained from local stations in Japan as well as from global infrasound stations show the importance of data fusion in detecting the generated meteor shock waves and explosive yield. The frequency-wavenumber (F–k) method is used to determine the back-azimuth and arrival times of the shock wave for the array stations. Moreover, the study focuses on detailed steps for yield estimation by using the period-yield relation, which depends on the duration of maximum energy. The shock wave period was calculated in the time and frequency domains. The optical observation results indicated the meteor trajectory with a location at 30.87° N, 131.94° E and an altitude of approximately 26.1 km, in high agreement compared to the location reported by the NASA Center for Near-Earth Object Studies (CNEOS; 30.9° N, 131.8° E) and an altitude of 27.5 km. Moreover, the yield calculated from the infrasound observation matched the reported CNEOS yield of 1.6 kt, compared to the average yield results from the time domain and frequency domain, which were 1.62 ± 1.17 kt and 1.61 ± 0.91 kt, respectively. Hence, integrating the seismic, infrasound, and optical observations contributed to precisely locating the meteor and determining the shockwave explosive yield. presentations.presentation_title: Trajectory Reconstruction and Analysis Of The August 2025 Fireball Over Japan Using Multi-Station Optical Data
presentations.abstract: On August 19 th , 2025, a fireball illuminated the sky over southern Japan and was rendered among the most energetic meteors recorded in the region in recent decades. Accurate reconstruction of a fireball’s trajectory is essential for constraining meteoroid physical properties and improving impact hazard assessments. The fireball trajectory was found using multi-station high-sensitivity video observations which were calibrated using SkyFit2 from the Raspberry Pi Meteor Station (RMS) software suite. Calibrated observations were combined using WesternMeteorPyLib (WMPL), an open-source meteor-physics library. Intersecting planes and line-of-sight methods were used to calculate the flight path which spans approximately 4s, with an apparent zenith angle of ~32°. The path terminates at an altitude extrapolated to be 26.1 kilometers (km), compared to an altitude of 27.5 km estimated by NASA’s Center for Near-Earth Object Studies (CNEOS), with a difference of 1.4 km. Extrapolation of the trajectory to the reported time of peak brightness (14:08:48 UTC) accounted for bending due to gravity, which is non-negligible for long-duration fireballs (≥4s). The calculated endpoint of the flight path revealed a difference 0.03° in latitude and a difference of 0.14° in longitude with an angular separation of 0.12° between the derived coordinates (30.87°N, 131.94°E) and the coordinates from the CNEOS database (30.9°N, 131.8°E). Velocity at time of peak brightness was calculated to be 19.2 kms -1 compared to 19.6 kms -1 as reported by CNEOS. This variance can be attributed to differing observational geometries and modeling assumptions. Angular residuals and the root-mean-square-deviation (RMSD) from these residuals were used to validate the trajectory. The RMSD for Shikoku and Kyushu are 1.1 and 1.7 arcminutes (i.e., 0.02° and 0.03°), respectively. This study demonstrates the effectiveness of combining multi-station video observations for fireball trajectory reconstruction.

presentations.presentation_title: Gravity Modeling of Irregular Small Body Through a Dynamic Lagrangian Mascon Framework
presentations.abstract: IntroductionAccurate gravity modeling is essential for spacecraft navigation around irregular small bodies. Classical spherical-harmonic representations deteriorate in the near field, while polyhedral and traditional mascon models require fixed discretizations or strong assumptions on density homogeneity[1]. We introduce a Dynamic Lagrangian mascon framework in which particle locations and populations evolve during learning, enabling adaptive resolution without relying on a predefined spatial mesh.MethodOur approach treats the mascon distribution as a dynamic system that self-organizes under a self-supervised, deep-learning-based optimization framework through three core Lagrangian operators.Split: The Split operator adaptively increases spatial resolution by identifying particles associated with large gravity residuals and subdividing them, thereby resolving high-frequency mass anomalies and complex internal structures.Clone:The Clone operator regulates local mass magnitude by duplicating particles at fixed locations, allowing dense regions to be modeled without increasing geometric complexity.Prune: The Prune operator enforces sparsity and physical consistency by removing statistically insignificant particles or elements that migrate outside the body’s volume, acting as a regularization mechanism that improves computational efficiency and interpretability.Together, these operators form an adaptive particle system that concentrates modeling capacity only where required by the gravity data.Preliminary ResultsThe framework was validated on asteroid (433) Eros [2]. Under equal particle counts and comparable acceleration-error levels, the proposed strategy exceeds GeodesyNet[3] and MasconCube[4] in near-field gravity regression while maintaining competitive recovery of low-degree Stokes coefficients. On a single NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU, GeodesyNet requires about 90 minutes of training, MasconCube 225 seconds, and our method roughly 90 seconds, yielding a 2.5× speedup over MasconCube and an approximately 60× reduction relative to GeodesyNet. For spherical-harmonic degrees up to 6, relative Stokes-coefficient errors below 10 -5 are obtained, comparable to MasconCube.

presentations.presentation_title: Observations of Asteroid (98943) Torifune by Jaxa’s Hayabusa2#
presentations.abstract: JAXA’s Hayabusa2#, the extended mission of its nominal mission Hayabusa2, will pass through the flyby target (98943) Torifune on July 5, 2026. The asteroid is reported to have an equivalent diameter of about 450 m and be elongated. The spin period is about 5 hr, and no tumbling state has been detected. The taxonomic class is likely Sq-type, though the possibility of an L-type class was also reported in the literature. Hayabusa2#’s current plan is for the spacecraft to approach the target at an encounter speed of about 5.25 km/s, with an expected closest approach of 1-10 km. By employing an approach that fixes the spacecraft’s orientation, the mission will achieve high-resolution imaging despite its limitations. The mission will employ the Optical Navigation Cameras (ONCs), Thermal Imager (TIR), Near Infrared Spectrometer (NIRS3), and Light Detection and Ranging (LIDAR) instrument to obtain scientific data as much as possible and capture the target asteroid’s formation and evolution processes. This presentation summarizes the preliminary analysis of Torifune using Hayabusa2#’s flyby data.

presentations.presentation_title: Dust Trails Origin of Ursid Meteor Shower Outbursts
presentations.abstract: The Ursid meteor shower is one of the established meteor showers. It is usually a minor shower with low activity; however, occasional outbursts have been recorded in the past, such as in 1981 and 1986. The parent body of the Ursids is comet 8P/Tuttle, but these outbursts show little correlation with the perihelion returns of the parent comet. On 22 December 2025, an outburst of the Ursids was observed across Japan. This activity was also captured by the Subaru-Asahi Star Camera, which provides a live stream from the Maunakea site in Hawaii. Prior to the event, our numerical simulations indicated that a dust trail ejected from the parent comet in AD 1117 would approach the Earth. However, because the encounter conditions were unfavorable, the expected activity was judged to be very weak. Contrary to this expectation, the observed outburst was stronger than anticipated. In this presentation, we summarize the relationship between past Ursid outbursts and associated dust trails, and discuss the resonant structures of these dust trails with Jupiter, including mean-motion resonances such as 13:15 and 15:17. We also report predictions for future outbursts of the Ursids.

presentations.presentation_title: The Quartz Quandary of WASP-17b: Extracting Maximal Information from Silicate Cloud Features in Exoplanet Spectra Through Various Modeling and Laboratory Techniques
presentations.abstract: Silicate clouds in the form of sub-micron sized crystalline SiO 2 particles have been found on the dayside of the hot Jupiter HD 189733b (T equ = 1200K) and limb of WASP-17b (T equ = 1800K). Best efforts to fit the WASP-17b transmission spectra have resulted in a modeled SiO2 feature that is offset to the actual MIRI LRS data. In this presentation, I will discuss the various methods used to better fit the silicate feature and extract information from its spectral shape. We first explore the orientation of crystalline silicate aerosols, whose non-isotropic interaction with radiation can form phenomena, like sun dogs, that can be observed in hot Jupiters in the mid-infrared and allows us to directly probe whether or not aerosols are coupled to strong winds. We then explore how SiO 2 has multiple stable low-pressure, high-temperature polymorphs that may be found in hot Jupiter atmospheres. These polymorphs all have different absorption features and specific thermal stability regimes that can be leveraged to trace the thermal history of the atmosphere from where a polymorph formed to where they are observed. Finally, we present new temperature-dependent transmittance measurements of SiO 2 samples taken with modern laboratory techniques at the Hot Environments Lab (HEL) at NASA GSFC. We find that the inclusion of temperature dependence, polymorph, crystalline vs amorphous, and synthetic vs natural all have a large effect in the fitted SiO 2 absorption feature, as well as find that the absorption feature is a strong probe of instantaneous temperature, opening the doorway for further interpretation of the 3D nature of exoplanet observations. Looking ahead, we are revisiting WASP-17b with two additional MIRI transits in the JWST Cycle 4 Program, where these upcoming datasets will be the perfect testbed for our new lab data and modeling techniques we’ve developed.

presentations.presentation_title: A Novel Retrieval Technique to Probe Photochemical and Mixing Processes in Exoplanets
presentations.abstract: The recent detections of photochemically produced SO2 in the atmospheres of the exoplanets WASP-39b, WASP-107b, and GJ 3470b, among others, have made the ubiquity of photochemistry in exoplanet atmospheres clear. Together with mixing processes, photochemistry can drastically alter molecular abundances from equilibrium predictions. In these cases, chemical equilibrium retrievals can deliver inaccurate constraints on bulk properties such as the C/O ratio and metallicity. In this presentation, we introduce a method for conducting disequilibrium chemistry atmospheric retrievals using grids of models that include the effects of photochemistry and vertical mixing. We apply this method to the complete JWST transmission spectrum dataset for WASP-39b, deriving new constraints on the C/O ratio, metallicity, vertical mixing strength, temperature-pressure profile, and SO2 mixing ratio profile. We find promising agreement between our novel retrieval method and existing free retrieval-based and forward model-based analyses. In the future, we intend to make our method available to the community as an addition to the open-source retrieval code POSEIDON, as disequilibrium chemistry atmospheric retrievals will become an increasingly critical tool in accurately interpreting exoplanet spectra.

presentations.presentation_title: Detectability of Escaping Atmosphere from Terrestrial Exoplanets with Water Vapor Atmosphere by Ultraviolet Transit Spectroscopy
presentations.abstract: Terrestrial exoplanets orbiting low-mass stars are primary targets in current habitable exoplanet exploration. Although atmospheric observations are underway to estimate the habitability of such planets, no atmosphere has been detected due to their small radii. In this context, ultraviolet spectroscopy is expected to be a breakthrough in atmospheric observations of these planets, as it provides large transit features and direct insights into atmospheric escape.On water-rich terrestrial planets inside the inner edge of the habitable zone, the runaway greenhouse effect is expected to evaporate the oceans. This results in the formation of water vapor atmospheres. In addition, low-mass stars emit strong X-ray and extreme ultraviolet (XUV) radiation over geological timescales. Consequently, hydrogen and oxygen atoms produced by the photodissociation of water vapor in the upper atmosphere would undergo hydrodynamic escape due to XUV heating. Future space telescope missions with UV detectors, such as LAPYUTA (JAXA) and HWO (NASA), would provide a chance to detect these atmospheres and enhance our understanding of atmospheric evolution through UV transit observations.In this study, we investigated the transmission spectral shapes and transit depths of the escaping atmosphere around a water-rich terrestrial exoplanet. Our model considers stellar and planetary gravity, radiation pressure, and photoionization, assuming intense UV environments around low-mass stars. Our simulations show that the spatial and velocity distributions of hydrogen atoms in the environment around the habitable zone of low-mass stars are different from those of observed close-in gas giants. This is because outward forcing involving radiation pressure is weak around low-mass stars. In this presentation, we will demonstrate how variations in parameters, such as XUV radiation intensity, the radiation pressure strength, and stellar radius, affect the shape of transmission spectra and discuss the feasibility of future observations based on stellar and planetary conditions.

presentations.presentation_title: Jwst Observations of the Cornerstone Temperate Sub-neptune K2-18 B
presentations.abstract: Earth-temperature, sub-Neptune-sized exoplanets are now within reach for detailed atmospheric characterization with JWST, with K2-18 b being one of the first to receive repeated observations. Initial observations revealed an H 2 -dominated atmosphere rich in CH 4 with moderate evidence for CO 2 . We have conducted additional JWST observations to capture new transmission spectra of the planet using NIRSpec’s G235H and G395H grisms. The resulting high-precision transmission spectrum robustly detects both CH 4 and CO 2 , precisely measuring their abundances and firmly establishing the planet’s water-rich nature. The planet could have either a thick envelope with >10% H 2 O by volume or a thin atmosphere above a liquid-water ocean. The spectrum reveals no detectable H 2 O, NH 3 , or CO. The absence of atmospheric water vapor suggests an efficient cold trap, while the nondetections of NH 3 and CO support the scenario of a small H 2 -rich atmosphere overlying a liquid reservoir. However, alternative models that include these gases can also reproduce the spectrum within uncertainties and offsets, highlighting the need for deeper observations. This unprecedented dataset offers critical insights into K2-18 b’s internal structure and informs an updated roadmap for characterizing temperate sub-Neptunes, advancing our understanding of their atmospheric properties and potential habitability.

presentations.presentation_title: Capture the Geomechanical Property in the Shallow Subsurface of the Moon Based on Waveform Analysis
presentations.institution: Indian Institute of Technology (Indian School of MInes), Dhanbad
presentations.abstract: Understanding geomechanical properties is a significant part of understanding subsurface geology of the Moon. Tectonic activities are captured in the waveform distribution, and these distributions are utilized to develop a suitable geomechanical model of the subsurface formation. The changes in the waveform are related to changes in the velocity through the formation, whereas these velocity distributions relate to the estimation of geomechanical parameters. Significant undulations and roughness are observed in the Moon’s surface, which are the outcome of the major tectonic activities. Separate and multiple tectonic regimes exhibit distinct geomechanical characterisation. The data received from the Moon indicate ongoing, frequent tectonic activity due to moonquakes. The current study has been carried out based on the analysis of waveforms generated due to moonquakes. The velocity components, such as P & S waves, are identified from the waveform. A stochastic approach was adopted to develop a velocity model to reduce the uncertainty. A model-based empirical relationship was used to estimate various pressure components along with elastic parameters. The distribution pattern of the estimated geomechanical properties develops the understanding of the plate tectonics in the shallow subsurface of the Moon. This understanding is highly significant for further development of the Moon’s surface, including identification of possible zones of key energy resources or mineral exploration.

presentations.presentation_title: Mineralogy and Texture of a Mafic-rich Lunar Surface Rock Observed at the Slim Landing Site
presentations.abstract: Previous remote-sensing data obtained by the SELENE (Kaguya) Spectral Profiler found exposures with olivine-rich spectral features, globally distributed on the lunar surface [1]. Their distribution and composition suggest that these olivine-rich exposures possibly originated from the mantle that is excavated by basin-forming impacts. Japanese lunar explorer, Smart Lander for Investigating Moon (SLIM) landed on outside the southern rim of Theophilus (11.4◦ S, 26.4◦ E), where olivine exposures were identified [2]. In this study we investigated a mafic-rich rock by using data obtained by Multi-Band Camera (MBC) on the SLIM. The MBC has a telescopic optical system capable of near-infrared high-spatial-resolution observation in 10 bands from 750 nm to 1,650 nm, and its spatial resolution is 1.1 mm/pixel at 10 m for mineralogical-scale observation and textual analysis. The analyzed rock consists of approximately equal amounts of olivine and plagioclase clasts and having the coarser rock texture (average clast size is roughly 6 times larger) than those of a previously known lunar rock sample having the coarsest rock texture (Apollo 76535). We classified the rock as a troctolite and because the rock contains much larger clast than Apollo 76535, tits rock texture suggest that the rock formed at a much slower cooling rate than Apollo 76535. Apollo sample 76535 is estimated as one of the most slowly cooled lunar samples [3]. Therefore, the much slower cooling-rate suggested for the analyzed rock may implies a previously unreported lunar internal process during formation of this troctolite. [1] Yamamoto et al. (2010), Nature GeoSci. 3, 533-536. [2] Ohtake et al. (2025), 56 th LPSC, abstract # 3090. [3] Borg et al. (2017), G.C.A., 201, 377-391.

presentations.presentation_title: Overview of the Lunar Polar Exploration (LUPEX) Project: Development Status of Mission Instruments, Observation Strategy and Scenario.
presentations.abstract: Lunar Polar Region Exploration (LUPEX) is a joint exploration project between the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA). Main objective is estimation of lunar water volume and quality. To achieve this, obtain the ground truth data of water qualities, quantity, distributions and surrounding environmental data by LUPEX rover and its mission instruments and using its to constraint and update of water concentration mechanism. The ultimate objective is to evaluate the usefulness of this water ice as a resource for future lunar exploration and development.The basic strategy of LUPEX observations involves the two distinct stages The first, course observations (scan observations) employing the rover's onboard instruments within a predetermined observation area in proximity to the landing site. Based on the acquired data, locations for detailed observations (i.e. drilling analysis) are selected, followed by drilling to obtain and analyse regolith samples as second step. Prior to launch, selection of observation areas is conducted. It is essential to choose locations where water ice is present, and where broad information can be obtained regarding the origin, age, and environmental conditions of the water ice rich layer/region.This presentation will show an overview of the current status of the development of mission instruments system. It also reports the details of the observation operations sequences, the selection of candidate landing sites and exploration areas, and the current status of analysis of existing data of candidate sites.

presentations.presentation_title: Geological Characterization of the Freundlich-Sharonov Basin: Implications for ISRU on the Moon
presentations.abstract: The Freundlich-Sharonov Basin (FS Basin) is a pre-Nectarian/Nectarian impact basin (diameter ~600km) on the lunar farside (18.35ºN, 175.2ºE) [1, 2]. It hosts spatially restricted and isolated volcanic patches. In this study, we conduct a detailed geological characterization of the FS Basin and evaluate its in-situ resource utilization (ISRU) potential through integrated morphological, chronological, and compositional analyses using datasets from the Chandrayaan-1, Kaguya, and LRO missions. Morphological analysis reveals the presence of a previously unrecognized inner depression ring (diameter ~192km), as evidenced by elevated topography, spatially aligned magmatic intrusions, orthopyroxenes, and purest anorthosite (PAN) exposures. Compositional investigation shows that the volcanic eruptions are dominated by low-Ti, high-alumina basalts with high-Ca pyroxene-rich mineralogy. Crater chronology reveals at least two volcanic episodes at ~3.4-3.3Ga and ~2.1Ga, demonstrating late-stage volcanism on the farside. The high-alumina basalts (~16-24wt% Al 2 O 3 ) within the FS Basin could be an important ISRU feedstock for aluminium and oxygen extraction, which can be used to source, in-situ, structural components, instrument fabrication, life support, and propulsion requirements. In addition, the central farside location of the FS Basin, shielded from terrestrial radio-frequency interference, and the presence of mare units with relatively uniform topography free of magnetic anomalies make this site a compelling target for farside operations. For e.g., Lacus Luxuriae, within the basin, is the only mare region categorized as a first-tier potential FarView build site for a low-frequency radio observatory [3, 4]. Overall, this study offers important geological context for understanding the volcano-tectonic evolution of the FS Basin and its relevance for future exploration and ISRU applications.[1] Orgel C. et al. (2018) JGR Planets, 123, 748-762. [2] Neumann G. A. et al. (2015) Sci. Adv. 1, e1500852. [3] Polidan R. S. (2024) Adv. Space Res., 74(1), 528-546. [4] Srivastava, private communications (2022, 2023).

presentations.presentation_title: Time-dependent Modeling of the Lunar Helium Exosphere Driven by Solar Wind Variability
presentations.abstract: Helium is one of the most abundant species in the lunar exosphere and serves as a key tracer of solar wind–surface interactions. The lunar helium population arises from both exogenic and endogenic sources: implantation of solar wind alpha particles provides the dominant external supply, while radiogenic production within the lunar interior is thought to contribute a comparatively small and likely secondary component. Previous steady-state models have shown that the solar wind alpha flux accounts for the vast majority of exospheric helium, but these studies typically rely on time-averaged assumptions, such as a fixed 5-day exponential decay timescale. In this work, we develop a time-dependent global Monte Carlo model to investigate the dynamical response of the lunar helium exosphere to extreme variations in the solar wind. Our results quantify how rapid enhancements in the incident alpha flux modify the helium source rate and surface distribution. By explicitly modeling the delay between alpha particle implantation and the subsequent thermalization and release of helium atoms from the regolith, we reveal the finite “memory” of the exosphere to prior solar wind conditions. These results provide new constraints on atmospheric loss processes and on the efficiency of the lunar regolith in converting solar wind ions into a thermalized neutral exosphere.

presentations.presentation_title: Endurance: a Concept for a Long-Range Rover to Explore the Moon’s South Pole-Aitken Basin
presentations.institution: California Institute of Technology, Jet Propulsion Laboratory
presentations.abstract: Endurance is a concept for a long-range, highly autonomous, robotic lunar rover designed to explore the farside of the Moon and the largest and oldest impact basin: South Pole–Aitken (SPA). Endurance would traverse >2,000 kilometers, acquire in situ data, and collect up to 100 kg of samples for delivery to Artemis astronauts at the lunar south pole. This concept represents a new way to explore, combining next-generation rover autonomy and a powerful partnership between human and robotic explorers. Endurance would address long-standing planetary science questions and provide the “ground truth” for the early history of the Solar System, the lunar mantle, and the role of giant impact basins in planetary evolution.Endurance was initially conceived by the United States of America’s National Academies of Science, Engineering, and Medicine’s 2023–2032 Planetary Science and Astrobiology Decadal Survey. The Decadal Survey recommended Endurance as the highest priority new robotic mission for NASA’s Lunar Discovery and Exploration Program. In response to the recommendation, NASA initiated the SPA sample Return and eXploration (SPARX) Science Definition Team (SDT) in early 2025. SDTs are a necessary step for NASA’s strategic science missions and often inform future mission and instrument development. The SPARX SDT is anticipated to complete its report in Spring 2026.In parallel to the SDT, NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), has continued technical development of the Endurance concept, focusing on key challenges for the mission including power and thermal designs, traverse planning, and autonomy. JPL has developed a new half-scale rover test platform to test these technologies, ERNEST (Exploration Rover for Navigating Extreme and Sloped Terrains), and successfully performed field test with autonomous, high-speed, day/night driving.In this presentation, we will present the status of Endurance. Information presented here is pre-decisional and provided for planning and discussion purposes only.

presentations.presentation_title: Cloud-top Circulation of Venus Studied Using the Denoised Thermal Infrared Images
presentations.abstract: Thermal infrared images captured by Longwave Infrared Camera (LIR) onboard Akatsuki provide valuable information about the dynamics of Venusian atmosphere. LIR successfully detects thermal emission in a waveband 8-12 μm from the cloud deck of Venus on dayside and nightside with equal quality [1] . However, the noise in the infrared images prevents further investigation of the Venusian atmosphere. We adopted a novel algorithm to enhance the image quality of the thermal infrared data (LIR) obtained by Akatsuki. The algorithm, named The Block-Matching and 3D Filtering (BM3D), is a non-local, adaptive, nonparametric filtering methodology based on a sparse representation in the frequency domain, combining the advantages of spatial filtering and frequency filtering to achieve better denoising effect [2] . We deduced the wind velocities by tracking the cloud patterns in these denoised images [3] . The mean flow at the cloud top level is analyzed, indicating a superrotation of ~95 m s -1 and a weak mean meridional flow. Long-term variations of the mean wind structure are studied, implying a synchronization between wind and temperature. The contributions of thermal tides and transient waves to the momentum budget are evaluated, showing their distinct roles in maintaining the superrotation. presentations.presentation_title: Identification and Characterization of the Topside Bulge of the Venusian Ionosphere
presentations.abstract: Venus lacks an intrinsic magnetic field, allowing the solar wind to interact directly with its ionosphere and drive significant variability in plasma structure. Earlier missions (Mariner, Venera, and Pioneer Venus Orbiter) reported a recurring localized enhancement in electron density at ~160–200 km altitude, commonly referred to as a “topside bulge.” In this study, we investigate the occurrence and morphology of this bulge using more than 200 dayside electron density profiles from the Venus Radio Science (VeRa) experiment on board Venus Express. We apply an automated, gradient-based classification approach to identify bulge signatures and categorize observed morphology in a quantitative, reproducible manner¹. Three bulge types are defined: (1) a distinct secondary peak above the main V2 layer, (2) a shoulder-like enhancement near bulge altitudes, and (3) a subtle bulge detectable through residual analysis after subtracting a Chapman-layer fit to the V2 peak. The bulge is detected in over 80% of the analyzed profiles, with higher occurrence during low solar activity and at lower solar zenith angles (SZA). Type 1 morphologies occur only at low latitudes (within ±40°). The bulge peak altitude shows a negative correlation with SZA, suggesting that thermospheric cooling toward the terminator plays an important role in controlling bulge altitude. Overall, the occurrence patterns and morphological characteristics support the interpretation that the bulge is strongly influenced by external drivers, such as solar wind interaction, rather than being solely produced by local photochemical processes. presentations.presentation_title: Modeling Gravity Wave Propagation in the Venusian Upper Atmosphere Under Varying Background Wind Conditions
presentations.abstract: Planetary atmospheres exhibit strong vertical coupling driven by atmospheric waves that transport energy and momentum from the lower atmosphere to the upper atmosphere and ionosphere. Among these, gravity waves play a particularly important role in shaping the structure and variability of planetary ionospheres. On Venus, recent observations suggest that gravity waves can influence ionospheric plasma distributions; however, key uncertainties remain regarding their propagation through a highly variable background atmosphere and their ability to reach ionospheric heights under different local time conditions. In particular, while thermospheric winds are known to be predominantly day-to-night and strongly dependent on local time, their role in modulating gravity wave transmission and neutral–ionospheric coupling is not well constrained. To address this problem, we develop a linear neutral atmospheric model for Venus by solving the fluid dynamical equations of mass, momentum, and energy conservation under Venusian conditions. Gravity wave propagation is examined for a range of wave parameters, and the effects of background winds are explicitly included to investigate wave behavior under different local time conditions. A parametric analysis of stationary and non-stationary gravity waves reveals that afternoon local time conditions are favorable for the propagation of stationary waves to ionospheric altitudes. For non-stationary waves with zonal phase velocities similar to the background zonal wind velocity in the middle cloud region, unidirectional wind profiles without critical levels enhance vertical wave penetration. Larger vertical wavelength waves experience less dissipation, and higher latitudes preferentially allow the propagation of higher phase-speed waves. These results are validated through comparison with radio occultation observations, supporting the role of gravity waves and background winds in controlling ionospheric variability on Venus.

presentations.presentation_title: Formation of V0 Layer in Venus’ Nightside Ionosphere Induced by SEP Events
presentations.abstract: The V0 layer in the Venusian ionosphere is a sporadic electron density peak detected on both the dayside and nightside by radio occultation. Using observations from the Venus Express Radio Science experiment (VEx/VeRa) and the Akatsuki Radio Science experiment (Akatsuki/RS), we find that the peak altitude of the dayside V0 layer is typically located near 110 km, whereas the nightside V0 peak is found near 120 km. However, the formation mechanisms of both remain unclear, and studies focusing on the nightside are still relatively scarce (Tripathi et al., 2024). We investigate the relationship between nightside V0 occurrence and solar activity, particularly solar energetic particle (SEP) events. Magnetic field variations measured by the Venus Express magnetometer (VEx/MAG) are used to characterize solar activity, and 3-day and 5-day windows prior to each occultation are examined for correlations between nightside V0 events and enhanced field fluctuations. The 3-day window yields p = 0.0004, indicating a significant association, whereas the 5-day window gives p ≈ 0.05. We further analyze STEREO-A data from 2–21 March 2011, when it was closely connected to Venus along the Parker spiral, to utilize the electron and proton fluxes as inputs of solar energetic particles (SEPs) to the Particles TRansport In Planetary atmosphere (PTRIP) model (Nakamura et al., 2022). The CO₂⁺ production rates simulated by PTRIP are then fed into the Photochemical and RadiatiOn Transport Model for Extensive USe (PROTEUS) to compute the peak altitude and density of the SEP-induced electron density enhancement. The modeled peaks compare well with the nightside V0 layer derived from VEx/VeRa, supporting SEPs as an important contributor to V0 formation and providing a basis for further studies of Venusian ionospheric dynamics and chemistry.
