presentations.presentation_title: Venus Cloud Structure Derived from Comparisons of Akatsuki Long-wave Infrared and Radio Science Measurements
presentations.institution: Jet Propulsion Laboratory/California Institute of Technology
presentations.abstract: Thermal infrared measurements with the Longwave Infrared Camera (LIR) on Akatsuki have revolutionized our understanding of Venus’ atmosphere with the discovery of stationary waves and the characterization of thermal tides. LIR predominantly measures the emission from mode 2 clouds of Venus’ cloud layer in the 8-12 μm wavelength range. Hence, its vertical sensitivity depends on the atmospheric cloud structure. We use vertical profiles of temperature derived from Akatsuki Radio Science measurements to calculate the expected brightness temperature in LIR measurements, varying the assumed cloud structure. We compare the calculated brightness temperatures with measured brightness temperatures from nearly coincident LIR observations. A total of 1309 pairs of Radio Science profiles with overlapping LIR images were analyzed. We find that a cloud top altitude around 65 km and a cloud scale height of 3.2 km for mode 2 clouds yields good agreement between measured and calculated brightness temperatures at low latitudes. The cloud top altitude decreases towards higher latitudes. Comparisons with cloud top altitudes derived from Akatsuki IR2 observations at 2.02 μm show reasonable agreement at mid- and low latitudes when the difference in measurement wavelength is considered. The derived cloud structure can be used as a priori to retrieve atmospheric temperatures from the brightness temperatures measured by LIR, together with their weighting functions that give the vertical sensitivity of the measurement. The retrieval algorithm is based on the one for the Mars Climate Sounder investigation, which has been adapted for the Venus atmosphere. This provides atmospheric temperature maps of Venus from LIR imagery throughout the Akatsuki mission, which will expand our understanding of Venus’ weather and climate over what can be gained from images of brightness temperature alone and facilitate the assimilation of LIR data into General Circulation Models. We will present near-final results of this study.

presentations.presentation_title: Global Distribution of Gravity Waves in the Venusian Middle Atmosphere Revealed by Radio Occultation
presentations.abstract: Atmospheric gravity waves are thought to play crucial roles in the vertical transport of energy and momentum in the atmospheres of the planets, including Venus. Venusian gravity waves have been extensively studied with radio occultation observations in NASA's Magellan mission, ESA's Venus Express mission, and JAXA's Akatsuki mission. An increase in amplitude at high latitudes was observed and attributed to topographic effects or to a possible enhancement of cloud-level convection at high latitudes. The decay of the amplitude with height was also observed and attributed to radiative damping. In order to fully understand the sources and dissipation processes of gravitational waves and quantitatively understand the role of gravity waves, the detailed distribution of waves over wide latitude and altitude ranges and its wavelength dependence need to be known. In this study, we explore the meridional distribution of gravity waves for different vertical wavelengths, including those less than 1 km, using the radio occultation data taken in the Akatsuki and Venus Express missions and analyzed with Full Spectrum Inversion. We found that the meridional distribution is qualitatively similar across the wavelength ranges. The temperature amplitude is relatively large at 60–70 km altitudes, especially at high latitudes. The amplitude increases with altitude above 75 km at low latitudes. Such a meridional distribution resembles that of the static stability of the background atmosphere. The local time dependence in the low latitude shows a tendency that the amplitude increases during daytime around 60 km altitude, where the static stability is relatively high. The positive correlation between the temperature amplitude and the background static stability is explained by two mechanisms: a higher static stability leads to a higher temperature amplitude for the same wave energy flux, or the wave amplitude is limited by the saturation amplitude, which is larger for higher static stability.

presentations.presentation_title: Radio Sounding of the Venusian Atmosphere and Ionosphere with the RSE Experiment on Envision
presentations.abstract: The Radio Science Experiment on EnVision will perform extensive studies of the gravitational field but also Radio Occultations to sense the Venus atmosphere and ionosphere at a high vertical resolution of only a few hundred metres. These radio occultations provide electron density profiles in the ionosphere and profiles in the troposphere and mesosphere providing atmospheric density, temperature and pressure profiles in the upper troposphere and mesosphere. Additionally, they allow to study the H 2 SO 4 absorption in the Venus cloud layer. These measurements will allow to study short term changes in the atmosphere and ionosphere. EnVision will use two coherent frequencies (X- and Ka-band) to separate dispersive and nondispersive effects. This allows to distinguish between ionospheric wave structures and other noise induced effects in the ionosphere. The use of Ka-band allows to study the H 2 SO 4 absorption in the Venus cloud layer due to its high sensitivity to sulfuric acid absorption. The monitoring of the H 2 SO 4 content helps to detect signatures of possible volcanic activity. Ka-band is also sensitive to liquid H 2 SO 4 which allows (in combination with X-band) to distinguish between gaseous and liquid H 2 SO 4 absorption features on Venus for the very first time. The short orbital period of EnVision in combination with its near polar orbit allows to cover all latitudes, longitudes, local times and solar zenith angles on Venus. Especially short-term variations caused by atmospheric waves can be identified to study traveling or stationary small-scale atmospheric structures.

presentations.presentation_title: Impacts of the 2018 Global Dust Storm on Martian Thermosphere/ionosphere Waves Activities
presentations.abstract: n this study, we compare responses of the thermosphere and ionosphere to a planet encirclingdust event in 2018 (PEDE 2018) occurred at the beginning of June 2018, a rare event last observed in 2007.Using the data from NGIMS (Neutral Gas and Ion Mass Spectrometer) instrument onboard MAVEN (MarsAtmosphere and Volatile EvolutioN) spacecraft, we examine wave signatures and their spectral changes of threeneutral species (O, Ar, CO ) and three ion species (O+, O +, CO +). Compared to low‐dust period, the following 222salient features stand out: (a) Wave activities (amplitudes) are significantly enhanced in the neutral species, but with smaller enhancement in the ion species; (b) The apparent wavelengths in the neutrals shift and broaden from a range of 50–300 km to 80–400 km, with dominant wavelength shifting from 100 to 200 km; (c) The apparent wavelengths in the ions shift and broaden from a range of 80–300 km to 100–400 km, with dominant wavelength shifting from 150 km to 250–300 km; (d) The correlations among the wavelength distributions of various species are high with correlation coefficient above 0.57 during low‐dust period and above 0.69 during PEDE 2018. These observed changes in wave signatures likely reflect filtering effects caused by changes in the middle atmosphere circulation induced by the global dust storm.

presentations.presentation_title: Numerical Modeling of Homogeneous Nucleation of Water-ice Clouds in the Martian Atmosphere
presentations.abstract: Cloud formation by water vapor plays a central role in regulating vertical transport and atmospheric escape in planetary atmospheres. In the classical cold-trap paradigm, condensation in the lower atmosphere limits the upward transport of vapor. For Mars, this framework has mainly focused on heterogeneous nucleation on dust particles. However, recent solar occultation observations show persistent supersaturation of water vapor at altitudes of about 50 to 80 km, indicating that the cold trap does not always efficiently remove vapor.Although supersaturation can promote upward transport and hydrogen escape, observed saturation ratios are typically limited to about 50 to 70. This suggests the presence of a process that constrains extreme supersaturation. Rather than implying a failure of the cold-trap concept, this behavior points to cloud formation processes in the upper atmosphere that have not been fully considered.Previous studies have discussed homogeneous nucleation in the Martian upper atmosphere but have focused mainly on hexagonal ice, which is stable at low temperatures. However, its high surface tension strongly suppresses homogeneous nucleation under observed conditions. In contrast, metastable phases such as amorphous solid water have lower surface tension and may nucleate more efficiently.In this study, we apply a discrete-sectional aerosol microphysics model based on the General Dynamic Equation to simulate homogeneous nucleation and growth of water–ice particles under Martian upper atmospheric conditions. Simulations are conducted at temperatures between 164 and 175 K using profiles from the Mars Climate Database. The results show that efficient homogeneous nucleation occurs for amorphous solid water once the saturation ratio exceeds about 70, producing particles with radii of tens to hundreds of nanometers within seconds, whereas hexagonal ice shows negligible nucleation. These results indicate that homogeneous nucleation of metastable ice may play an important role in regulating supersaturation and reinforcing the Martian cold trap.

presentations.presentation_title: Improving the Representation of the CO2 Cycle in the Mars PCM
presentations.abstract: Our Mars Planetary Climate Model (Mars PCM, formely known as the LMD Global Climate Model) simulates all the details of the atmospheric environment of Mars. It is developped at LMD (Laboratoire de Meteorologie Dynamique, Paris, France) in close collaboration with several teams in Europe (LATMOS, France, University of Oxford, The Open University, the Instituto de Astrofisica de Andalucia), and with the support of ESA (European Space Agency) and CNES (French Space Agency). It is used to generate the Mars Climate Database (MCD), the latest version (version 6.1) of which was released in 2022. The reference version of the Mars PCM has been shown to correctly represent the Martian CO2 cycle and well match the pressure cycles recorded by landers and rovers at the surface of Mars. The main reason behind obtaining a reasonable seasonal evolution of the CO2 cycle is adequately accounting for the seasonal condensation and sublimation of CO2 at the poles. However this has so far been done with a simplification hypothesis that the CO2 slab at the surface is isothermal and at the CO2 frost point temperature of the atmosphere above it. In practice the CO2 slab can build up to thicknesses of the order of a meter. We have implemented a scheme to compute the thermal evolution of the slab, including the frost point dependency with pressure and interaction with the sub-surface heat flux. At AOGS we will report on the impact of this improvement on the modeled Martian CO2 cycle.

presentations.presentation_title: New Results on Dust Devils
presentations.institution: Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory
presentations.abstract: Dust devils are among the most prominent features of Mars surface meteorology and are of operational importance in that they can clean lander or rover solar arrays. The accumulated data from various Mars missions now gives a measure of dust devil activity and its variability at several sites. Notably, the InSight landing site at Elysium had many vortices detected in pressure and other data, but no visible dust devils seen in imaging. In contrast, the Perseverance landing site at Jezero has abundant dust activity, and indeed sand deposited on its deck by wind. A recent result documented electrostatic discharges on the rover, some coincident with dust devil encounters. Terrestrial field studies can give us a deeper understanding of dust devil phenomena, and I review some results from a number of in-situ measurement and timelapse camera campaigns.

presentations.presentation_title: Turbulence in the Stable and Convective Boundary Layer on Mars
presentations.abstract: The lowermost part of the Martian atmosphere, the planetary boundary layer (PBL), modulates the amount of matter, momentum, and heat exchanged between the planetary surface and its atmosphere. The dynamics of the Martian PBL are driven by turbulent mixing. We use the LMD mesoscale model for regions around several landed Mars missions to investigate the relationships between circulation, turbulence and the influence of global dust storm climatology. At sites of complex topography, we find that slope winds can lead to the formation of low-level jets, which weaken the nighttime stability through wind shear.
